items.q: A man walks 8 m to the east and then 6 m to the south. What is his eastward displacement?
items.explain:
The eastward displacement is the east component of the total displacement: only the 8 m walked east counts; the 6 m south has no east component.
Eastward displacement $=8\,\mathrm{m}$.

items.q: A man walks 8 m to the east and then 6 m to the south. What is the magnitude of his total displacement from the start?
items.explain:
Displacement is the straight line from start to end: $\sqrt{8^2+6^2}=\sqrt{100}=10\,\mathrm{m}$.
The path length (distance) is $8+6=14\,\mathrm{m}$, which is a different quantity.

items.q: A man walks 8 m to the east and then 6 m to the south. The total displacement points south of east by an angle of
items.explain:
$\tan\theta=\dfrac{6}{8}$, so $\theta=\arctan 0.75=36.9^\circ$ south of east.
$53.1^\circ$ is the angle from the south direction (the complement).

items.q: A runner completes exactly one lap of a 400 m track in 80 s. Her average velocity for the lap and her average speed are
items.explain:
Displacement for a full lap is $0$, so average velocity $=0/80=0$.
Distance is $400\,\mathrm{m}$, so average speed $=400/80=5\,\mathrm{m/s}$.

items.q: For a particle accelerating along a straight line, what is the definition of its velocity?
opts: Velocity is the rate of change of displacement
Velocity is distance divided by time
Velocity is the rate of change of distance
Velocity is displacement divided by time
items.explain:
Instantaneous velocity is $v=\mathrm{d}x/\mathrm{d}t$: the rate of change of displacement.
'Displacement divided by time' is only the average velocity over an interval, and anything built on distance is a speed.

items.q: Which of the following gives the acceleration of a body?
opts: the area under its displacement-time graph
the gradient of its velocity-time graph
the gradient of its displacement-time graph
the area under its velocity-time graph
items.explain:
$a=\mathrm{d}v/\mathrm{d}t$ is the gradient (slope) of the velocity-time graph.
The gradient of the displacement-time graph is the velocity, and the area under the velocity-time graph is the displacement.

items.q: A car accelerates at $5\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$ from rest for $10\,\mathrm{s}$. What is its speed at the end of the $10\,\mathrm{s}$?
items.explain:
$v=u+at=0+5\times10=50\,\mathrm{m/s}$.
$25\,\mathrm{m/s}$ is the average speed and $250\,\mathrm{m}$ would be the distance $\tfrac12at^2$: do not mix them up.

items.q: A racing car accelerates uniformly along a straight road. Marker posts are $100\,\mathrm{m}$ apart. The car passes one post at $10\,\mathrm{m/s}$ and the next at $20\,\mathrm{m/s}$. What is its acceleration?
items.explain:
No time is given, so use $v^2=u^2+2as$:
$a=\dfrac{v^2-u^2}{2s}=\dfrac{400-100}{200}=1.5\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$.
Check with the time: average speed $15\,\mathrm{m/s}$, $t=100/15=6.67\,\mathrm{s}$, $a=10/6.67=1.5\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$.

items.q: A metal ball hits a sand bed one second after it is released from rest and makes an impression $8.0\,\mathrm{mm}$ deep. Air resistance is negligible. What is the average deceleration of the ball in the sand?
items.explain:
Impact speed after $1\,\mathrm{s}$ of free fall: $v=gt=9.8\,\mathrm{m/s}$.
In the sand $v^2=2ad$ with $d=8.0\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m}$: $a=\dfrac{9.8^2}{2\times0.008}=6.0\times10^3\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$.
Forgetting the factor 2 gives $1.2\times10^4$.

items.q: A car decelerates at $5\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$ from an initial speed of $40\,\mathrm{m/s}$. What is its speed after $6\,\mathrm{s}$?
items.explain: $v=u+at=40-5\times6=10\,\mathrm{m/s}$ (the car is still moving: it stops only after $8\,\mathrm{s}$).

items.q: A car with a hole in its petrol tank loses a drop of petrol at a constant rate. The car travels at constant speed $2\,\mathrm{m/s}$ and the gap between two drops on the road is $50\,\mathrm{cm}$. What is the frequency of the drips?
items.explain:
Time between drops $T=\dfrac{d}{v}=\dfrac{0.50}{2}=0.25\,\mathrm{s}$, so $f=1/T=4\,\mathrm{Hz}$.
Remember to convert $50\,\mathrm{cm}=0.50\,\mathrm{m}$.

items.q: A robot shoots a ball vertically upwards at $30\,\mathrm{m/s}$. What distance does the ball travel in the first $5\,\mathrm{s}$? ($g=10\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$)
items.explain:
It rises for $t=v_0/g=3\,\mathrm{s}$ to $h=v_0^2/2g=45\,\mathrm{m}$, then falls for $2\,\mathrm{s}$: $\tfrac12g(2)^2=20\,\mathrm{m}$.
Distance travelled $=45+20=65\,\mathrm{m}$; the displacement is only $45-20=25\,\mathrm{m}$ above the start.

items.q: A runner accelerates constantly at $2\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$ for the first $4\,\mathrm{s}$ of a $100\,\mathrm{m}$ race and then keeps that speed to the finish. How long does the race take him?
items.explain:
Acceleration phase: $v=at=8\,\mathrm{m/s}$, $s_1=\tfrac12at^2=16\,\mathrm{m}$.
Constant-speed phase: $100-16=84\,\mathrm{m}$ at $8\,\mathrm{m/s}$ takes $10.5\,\mathrm{s}$.
Total $=4+10.5=14.5\,\mathrm{s}$.

items.q: A car starts from rest and accelerates uniformly. After $5.0\,\mathrm{s}$ its speed is $20.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$. What is its acceleration?
items.explain: $a=\dfrac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}=\dfrac{20.0}{5.0}=4.0\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$.

items.q: A car starts from rest and accelerates uniformly. After $5.0\,\mathrm{s}$ its speed is $20.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$. What is its speed after $2.0\,\mathrm{s}$?
items.explain: $a=4.0\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$, so $v=at=4.0\times2.0=8.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$.

items.q: A car starts from rest and accelerates uniformly. After $5.0\,\mathrm{s}$ its speed is $20.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$. What distance does it travel in the first $2.0\,\mathrm{s}$?
items.explain: $s=\tfrac12at^2=\tfrac12(4.0)(2.0)^2=8.0\,\mathrm{m}$; as a check the average speed is $(0+8)/2=4\,\mathrm{m/s}$, and $4\times2=8\,\mathrm{m}$.

items.q: A bus travels at $20\,\mathrm{m/s}$ when the driver sees an obstacle $120\,\mathrm{m}$ ahead. The reaction time is $0.6\,\mathrm{s}$ (the bus keeps its speed during it). How far does the bus travel during the reaction time?
items.explain: Constant speed: $s=vt=20\times0.6=12\,\mathrm{m}$.

items.q: After the brakes are applied the bus travels $100\,\mathrm{m}$ before stopping from $20\,\mathrm{m/s}$. What is the magnitude of its deceleration?
The bus (speed $20\,\mathrm{m/s}$, reaction time $0.6\,\mathrm{s}$, then $100\,\mathrm{m}$ of braking) is $120\,\mathrm{m}$ from the obstacle when the driver sees it. What happens?
opts: It stops exactly at the obstacle
It hits the obstacle: the stopping distance is $120\,\mathrm{m}$ or more
It stops $8\,\mathrm{m}$ before the obstacle: total stopping distance $112\,\mathrm{m}$
items.explain:
Total distance $=12+100=112\,\mathrm{m}<120\,\mathrm{m}$, so the bus stops $8\,\mathrm{m}$ short.
Forgetting the reaction distance would give $100\,\mathrm{m}$, i.e. $20\,\mathrm{m}$ spare, which is too optimistic.

items.q: In a speed trap two pressure strips are $120\,\mathrm{m}$ apart on a road with a limit of $85\,\mathrm{km/h}$. A driver at $110\,\mathrm{km/h}$ on the first strip slows down at once. What constant deceleration is needed so that his average speed between the strips just equals the limit?
items.explain:
Convert: $110\,\mathrm{km/h}=30.56\,\mathrm{m/s}$, $85\,\mathrm{km/h}=23.61\,\mathrm{m/s}$.
Time between strips at the limit: $t=120/23.61=5.08\,\mathrm{s}$. For constant deceleration $\bar v=(v_1+v_2)/2=23.61$, so $v_2=16.67\,\mathrm{m/s}$.
$a=\dfrac{v_1-v_2}{t}=\dfrac{13.89}{5.08}=2.73\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$. Check: $\dfrac{v_1^2-v_2^2}{2d}=2.73$.

items.q: A car of length $3.5\,\mathrm{m}$ overtakes a lorry of length $17.0\,\mathrm{m}$. The time is measured from the moment the front of the car is level with the rear of the lorry until the rear of the car is one full car length ahead of the lorry's front. The car is $8.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$ faster than the lorry. How long is this overtaking time $T$?
items.explain:
Relative to the lorry the car must move forward by the lorry length plus its own length (to clear the lorry) plus one more car length: $17.0+3.5+3.5=24.0\,\mathrm{m}$.
$T=\dfrac{24.0}{8.0}=3.0\,\mathrm{s}$.

items.q: The graph shows the velocity of a cyclist along a straight road. What is her displacement during the whole $14\,\mathrm{s}$?
items.explain:
Displacement = area under the $v$-$t$ graph = triangle $+$ rectangle $+$ triangle
$=\tfrac12(4)(8)+(6)(8)+\tfrac12(4)(8)=16+48+16=80\,\mathrm{m}$.
$8\times14=112$ would ignore the speeding up and slowing down.

items.q: A body falls from rest through air. Which statement about its acceleration is correct?
opts: It increases because the speed increases
It decreases as the speed increases and tends to zero at the terminal velocity
It becomes negative once the body is moving fast
It stays equal to $g$ the whole time
items.explain: Air resistance grows with speed. The net force $mg-F_{\text{drag}}$ shrinks, so $a$ falls from $g$ towards $0$; at the terminal velocity $F_{\text{drag}}=mg$ and $a=0$.

items.q: A speed-time graph of a falling object is a straight line through the origin with gradient $9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$ that never levels off. Which statement describes it best?
opts: The object rises and then falls
The object drops through air and reaches terminal velocity
The object is thrown downwards through air
The object drops through vacuum (free fall)
items.explain: A straight line means constant acceleration $g$: no air resistance, i.e. free fall in vacuum. In air the graph would curve and flatten at the terminal velocity.

items.q: A falling object has velocity $0,\ 9.5,\ 15.0,\ 19.0,\ 21.5,\ 23.0,\ 23.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$ at $t=0,1,\dots,6\,\mathrm{s}$. What is its average acceleration between $t=1.0$ and $t=2.0\,\mathrm{s}$?
items.explain: $\bar a=\dfrac{15.0-9.5}{2.0-1.0}=5.5\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$. It is smaller than the $9.5\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$ of the first second because air resistance has grown.

items.q: For the same data, what is the terminal velocity of the object?
items.explain: The speed stops changing at $23.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$ (from $t=5\,\mathrm{s}$ on): the acceleration is $0$ and drag balances weight.

items.q: A stone is released from rest at the top of a $40\,\mathrm{m}$ tower. Air resistance is negligible ($g=10\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$). How long does the stone take to fall the last $10\,\mathrm{m}$?
items.explain:
Total fall time: $t=\sqrt{2h/g}=\sqrt{8}=2.83\,\mathrm{s}$.
Time to fall the first $30\,\mathrm{m}$: $\sqrt{6}=2.45\,\mathrm{s}$.
Last $10\,\mathrm{m}$: $2.83-2.45=0.38\,\mathrm{s}$. (It is not $\sqrt{2\cdot10/10}=1.4\,\mathrm{s}$: that would be falling $10\,\mathrm{m}$ from rest.)

items.q: An object drops from the top of a building and takes $5.0\,\mathrm{s}$ to reach the ground ($g=10\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$). Its speeds after $1.0$, $2.0$ and $5.0\,\mathrm{s}$ are
items.explain:
$v=gt$: $10$, $20$, $50\,\mathrm{m/s}$ (the speed grows linearly with time).
$5$, $10$, $25$ would be $\tfrac12gt$; $10,40,250$ would use $v\propto t^2$.

items.q: An object drops for $5.0\,\mathrm{s}$ with $g=10\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$. What is the height of the building?
items.explain: $h=\tfrac12gt^2=\tfrac12(10)(25)=125\,\mathrm{m}$. Check: average speed $=\tfrac12(0+50)=25\,\mathrm{m/s}$, and $25\times5=125\,\mathrm{m}$.

items.q: An object drops from rest with $g=10\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$. How far does it fall in the NEXT second, i.e. between $t=1\,\mathrm{s}$ and $t=2\,\mathrm{s}$?
items.explain:
In the first second: $\tfrac12(10)(1)^2=5\,\mathrm{m}$; in the first two seconds: $\tfrac12(10)(2)^2=20\,\mathrm{m}$.
Second second: $20-5=15\,\mathrm{m}$ (distances in successive seconds are in the ratio $1:3:5\ldots$).

items.q: A bullet is fired vertically upwards at $100\,\mathrm{m/s}$ ($g=10\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$). How long does it take for its speed to fall to zero?
items.explain: $v=v_0-gt=0\Rightarrow t=\dfrac{100}{10}=10\,\mathrm{s}$.

items.q: A bullet is fired vertically upwards at $100\,\mathrm{m/s}$ ($g=10\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$). What maximum height does it reach?
items.explain: $h=\dfrac{v_0^2}{2g}=\dfrac{10^4}{20}=500\,\mathrm{m}$. Check: average speed $50\,\mathrm{m/s}$ for $10\,\mathrm{s}$ gives $500\,\mathrm{m}$.

items.q: A bullet is fired vertically upwards at $100\,\mathrm{m/s}$. What is its average speed on the way up to the highest point?
items.explain: Uniform deceleration from $100$ to $0$: average speed $=\tfrac12(100+0)=50\,\mathrm{m/s}$ ($=500\,\mathrm{m}/10\,\mathrm{s}$).

items.q: A ball is thrown vertically upwards. At the highest point of its motion, what are its velocity and its acceleration (up is positive, air resistance negligible)?
items.explain: At the top the velocity is momentarily zero, but gravity still acts, so $a=-g$ all the way: the acceleration is the same at every stage.

items.q: A shell is fired from the ground with initial speed $1.70\times10^{3}\,\mathrm{m/s}$ at $55.0^\circ$ to the horizontal. Neglecting air resistance, what is its horizontal range?
items.explain:
$R=\dfrac{v_0^2\sin2\theta}{g}=\dfrac{(1.70\times10^{3})^2\sin110^\circ}{9.8}=2.77\times10^{5}\,\mathrm{m}$.
Check by integrating the equations of motion numerically: $R=2.77\times10^5\,\mathrm{m}$. (Unrealistic without air resistance, but that is the model.)

items.q: The same shell ($v_0=1.70\times10^{3}\,\mathrm{m/s}$, $55.0^\circ$) - for how long is it in the air?
items.explain:
$T=\dfrac{2v_0\sin\theta}{g}=\dfrac{2(1700)\sin55^\circ}{9.8}=284\,\mathrm{s}$.
Equivalent: $T=R/(v_0\cos\theta)=2.77\times10^5/975=284\,\mathrm{s}$.

items.q: A daredevil is shot from a cannon at $45.0^\circ$ with initial speed $25.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$. A net is $50.0\,\mathrm{m}$ away horizontally. At what height above the cannon must the net be placed?
items.explain:
Time to reach the net: $t=\dfrac{x}{v_0\cos\theta}=\dfrac{50}{17.68}=2.83\,\mathrm{s}$.
Height: $y=v_0\sin\theta\,t-\tfrac12gt^2=17.68(2.83)-4.9(2.83)^2=10.8\,\mathrm{m}$.
Same result from $y=x\tan\theta-\dfrac{gx^2}{2v_0^2\cos^2\theta}=50-39.2=10.8\,\mathrm{m}$.

items.q: Galileo drops one weight straight down from a $100\,\mathrm{m}$ tower and at the same instant throws an identical weight horizontally at $5\,\mathrm{m/s}$. How long after release does the horizontal one hit the ground? (Neglect air resistance.)
items.explain: The vertical motion is independent of the horizontal one: both fall from rest vertically, so $t=\sqrt{2h/g}=\sqrt{2\times100/9.8}=4.52\,\mathrm{s}$ for both. They land at the same time.

items.q: For the same throw (horizontal speed $5\,\mathrm{m/s}$, tower $100\,\mathrm{m}$), what horizontal distance does the second weight travel before landing?
items.explain: $x=v_xt=5\times4.52=22.6\,\mathrm{m}$.

items.q: A cannon on a $50\,\mathrm{m}$ high cliff fires a ball over the edge at $200\,\mathrm{m/s}$ at $30^\circ$ above the horizontal. How long is the ball in the air? (Neglect air resistance.)
items.explain:
Vertical motion (up positive): $y=h_0+v_0\sin\theta\,t-\tfrac12gt^2=0$, i.e. $50+100t-4.9t^2=0$.
Positive root: $t=\dfrac{100+\sqrt{100^2+4(4.9)(50)}}{2(4.9)}=20.9\,\mathrm{s}$.
$2v_0\sin\theta/g=20.4\,\mathrm{s}$ is the time for a launch from ground level: the extra $50\,\mathrm{m}$ of height adds time.

items.q: Two projectiles are launched from ground level with the same speed. The maximum height of projectile 1 is twice that of projectile 2. The launch angles satisfy
items.explain:
$h=\dfrac{v_0^2\sin^2\theta}{2g}$, so $h_1=2h_2$ gives $\sin^2\theta_1=2\sin^2\theta_2$, i.e. $\sin\theta_1=\sqrt2\sin\theta_2$.
(In the printed sheet the tangent option has theta2 on both sides: a typing slip. The sine relation is the correct one.)

items.q: A ball is projected and follows a parabolic path through its highest point T (air resistance negligible). What is true of the vertical component of its acceleration?
opts: It is the same at every point, $g$ downwards
It is greatest at the launch point
items.explain: Only gravity acts, so the acceleration is $g$ downwards at every instant of the flight, including the top.

items.q: At the highest point of a projectile's path (air resistance negligible), which statement is true?
items.explain: The horizontal velocity stays $v_0\cos\theta\neq0$ all the way, so kinetic energy and momentum are not zero at the top. There is no horizontal force, so the horizontal acceleration is zero.

items.q: A ball is kicked from level ground at $20\,\mathrm{m/s}$ at $30^\circ$ above the horizontal. What is its horizontal range? (Neglect air resistance, $g=9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$.)
items.explain:
$R=\dfrac{v_0^2\sin2\theta}{g}=\dfrac{20^2\sin60^\circ}{9.8}=35.3\,\mathrm{m}$.
Numerical integration of the flight gives the same range.

items.q: For a fixed launch speed on level ground and no air resistance, which launch angle gives the greatest range?

items.q: A ball is thrown horizontally at $12\,\mathrm{m/s}$ from the edge of a $20\,\mathrm{m}$ cliff. What is its speed when it hits the ground? ($g=9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$)
items.explain:
Vertical speed from energy/kinematics: $v_y=\sqrt{2gh}=\sqrt{2(9.8)(20)}=19.8\,\mathrm{m/s}$; horizontal stays $12\,\mathrm{m/s}$.
Speed $=\sqrt{12^2+19.8^2}=23.2\,\mathrm{m/s}$ (components add as vectors, not as numbers).

items.q: A car travels due east at $50\,\mathrm{km/h}$. Rain falls vertically relative to the Earth, but the traces on the side windows make $60.0^\circ$ with the vertical. What is the speed of the rain relative to the car?
items.explain:
In the car's frame the rain has a horizontal component $50\,\mathrm{km/h}$ (westwards) and the vertical component $v_y$ of the rain relative to Earth. The streaks make $60^\circ$ with the vertical, so $\sin60^\circ=\dfrac{50}{v_{rain/car}}$.
$v_{rain/car}=\dfrac{50}{\sin60^\circ}=57.7\,\mathrm{km/h}$.

items.q: A car travels due east at $50\,\mathrm{km/h}$. The traces of the rain on the side windows make $60.0^\circ$ with the vertical. What is the speed of the rain relative to the Earth (it falls vertically)?
items.explain: Vertical component stays the same in both frames: $\tan60^\circ=\dfrac{50}{v_y}\Rightarrow v_y=\dfrac{50}{\tan60^\circ}=28.9\,\mathrm{km/h}$ downwards.

items.q: An escalator is $20.0\,\mathrm{m}$ long; standing on it takes $50.0\,\mathrm{s}$ to ride from the bottom to the top. How long does it take a person who walks up the moving escalator at $0.500\,\mathrm{m/s}$ relative to the escalator?
items.explain:
Escalator speed: $20.0/50.0=0.400\,\mathrm{m/s}$. Walking in the same direction the speeds add: $0.400+0.500=0.900\,\mathrm{m/s}$.
$t=20.0/0.900=22.2\,\mathrm{s}$.

items.q: The same escalator ($20.0\,\mathrm{m}$, $0.400\,\mathrm{m/s}$ going up). A person walks DOWN the 'up' escalator at $0.500\,\mathrm{m/s}$ relative to it. How long does she take to reach the bottom?
items.explain:
Relative to the ground she moves down at $0.500-0.400=0.100\,\mathrm{m/s}$.
$t=20.0/0.100=200\,\mathrm{s}$.

items.q: A boat can move at $4.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$ relative to the water. It heads straight across a $100\,\mathrm{m}$ wide river whose current is $3.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$. How far downstream does it land?
items.explain:
Crossing time $t=W/v_b=100/4.0=25\,\mathrm{s}$ (only the component across the river matters).
Drift $=v_rt=3.0\times25=75\,\mathrm{m}$.
items.src: Generated, same style as: Mechanics tutorial Part 2, Q25-Q26 (relative velocity)

items.q: The same boat ($4.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$ relative to the water) heads straight across the $3.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$ current. What is its speed relative to the river bank?
items.explain: The two velocity components are perpendicular: $v=\sqrt{4.0^2+3.0^2}=5.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$.
items.src: Generated, same style as: Mechanics tutorial Part 2, Q25-Q26

items.q: Two trains approach each other on parallel straight tracks at $30\,\mathrm{m/s}$ and $20\,\mathrm{m/s}$. How fast does one train appear to move relative to the other?
items.explain: Opposite directions: relative speed $=30+20=50\,\mathrm{m/s}$.

items.q: An observer in a frame A sees an object B move with velocity $\vec v_{BA}$. In a frame C that moves with velocity $\vec v_{AC}$ relative to C the same object has velocity
items.explain: Velocities add through the intermediate frame: $\vec v_{BC}=\vec v_{BA}+\vec v_{AC}$ (Lecture: $\vec v_{PA}=\vec v_{PB}+\vec v_{BA}$).

items.q: Which of the following is NOT one of Newton's laws of motion?
opts: The rate of change of momentum of a body is proportional to the net force and takes place in the direction of the force
The total momentum of a system of interacting bodies remains constant provided no external force acts
A body continues at rest or in uniform motion in a straight line unless acted on by an external force
If body A exerts a force on body B, then B exerts an equal and opposite force on A
items.explain: Options 2, 3, 4 are the second, third and first laws. Conservation of momentum is a consequence of the second and third laws, not one of the three laws.

items.q: A body is falling freely under gravity. What is its rate of change of momentum equal to?
items.explain: $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}p}{\mathrm{d}t}=F_{\text{net}}$, and the only force is the weight $mg$.

items.q: The graph of the force $F$ exerted on a body against time $t$ is given. The area under the graph represents the change of which quantity of the body?
items.explain: Impulse $=\int F\,\mathrm{d}t=\Delta p$: the area under a force-time graph is the change in momentum.

items.q: A box is pushed across a horizontal floor at constant speed. If the push is stopped, the box will
opts: move at constant speed for a while and then slow down
items.explain: Friction was balancing the push. When the push is removed the net force is the friction alone, opposite to the motion, so the box decelerates at once ($a=\mu g$).

items.q: A box is pushed along a rough surface with constant acceleration. If the push is suddenly stopped, the box will
items.explain: Only friction (opposite to the velocity) acts now: the box decelerates until it stops. It cannot stop instantly because velocity cannot change discontinuously without an impulsive force.

items.q: A passenger in a car is thrown forward when the car brakes sharply. Which law explains this best?
opts: Newton's second law with a constant force
items.explain: The passenger's body tends to keep its original velocity (inertia) while the car slows down beneath it: first law.

items.q: A book rests on a table. The weight of the book and the normal force of the table on the book are equal and opposite. Are they an action-reaction pair (Newton's third law)?
opts: No, because the normal force is larger
No: they act on the same body and are different kinds of force
Yes: they are equal and opposite
Yes, because the book is at rest
items.explain: Third-law pairs act on DIFFERENT bodies and are of the same type. The reaction to the weight (Earth pulls the book) is the book pulling the Earth; the reaction to the normal force is the book pushing on the table.

items.q: A tractor of mass $1000\,\mathrm{kg}$ tows a trailer of mass $1000\,\mathrm{kg}$. The total resistance to motion is a constant $4000\,\mathrm{N}$ and one quarter of it acts on the trailer. They move at a constant speed of $6\,\mathrm{m/s}$. What force does the tow-bar exert on the tractor?
items.explain: Constant speed $\Rightarrow$ zero net force on each body. The trailer feels a resistance of $4000/4=1000\,\mathrm{N}$ forwards-opposing, so the tow-bar must pull it with $1000\,\mathrm{N}$; by the third law the bar pulls back on the tractor with $1000\,\mathrm{N}$.

items.q: A box of mass $2\,\mathrm{kg}$ moves at a constant $3\,\mathrm{m/s}$ when pushed horizontally with a $4\,\mathrm{N}$ force on a rough surface. What is its acceleration when the push is increased to $6\,\mathrm{N}$?
items.explain:
At constant speed friction equals the push: $f=4\,\mathrm{N}$.
Now $a=\dfrac{F-f}{m}=\dfrac{6-4}{2}=1\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$.

items.q: Three identical blocks P, Q and R are joined in a line by light strings on a smooth surface and a force of $30\,\mathrm{N}$ pulls P at the front. What are the tensions $T_1$ (between P and Q) and $T_2$ (between Q and R)?
items.explain:
Whole system: $a=30/(3m)=10/m$.
$T_2$ must accelerate only R: $T_2=m a=10\,\mathrm{N}$.
$T_1$ accelerates Q and R: $T_1=2ma=20\,\mathrm{N}$. The tension decreases away from the pulled end.
items.src: Generated, same style as: Mechanics tutorial Part 3, Q8

items.q: Two blocks X and Y of masses $m$ and $3m$ touch each other on a smooth horizontal surface. A force $F$ pushes X, which pushes Y. What is the magnitude of the force X exerts on Y?
items.explain: Common acceleration $a=F/(4m)$. Y feels only the contact force: $N=3m\,a=\dfrac{3F}{4}$.

items.q: A $40\,\mathrm{kg}$ mass sits on a rough bench; a $10\,\mathrm{kg}$ mass hangs from it over a light pulley. A friction force of $20\,\mathrm{N}$ opposes the motion of the $40\,\mathrm{kg}$ mass. What is the speed of the $10\,\mathrm{kg}$ mass $2\,\mathrm{s}$ after the system is released? ($g=10\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$)
items.explain:
Net driving force $=m_2g-f=100-20=80\,\mathrm{N}$ on a total mass $50\,\mathrm{kg}$: $a=1.6\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$.
$v=at=1.6\times2=3.2\,\mathrm{m/s}$.

items.q: A $40\,\mathrm{kg}$ mass on a smooth table is joined by a light string over a pulley to a hanging $10\,\mathrm{kg}$ mass. What is the speed of the hanging mass $2\,\mathrm{s}$ after release from rest? ($g=10\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$)
items.explain: $a=\dfrac{m_2g}{m_1+m_2}=\dfrac{100}{50}=2\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$; $v=at=4\,\mathrm{m/s}$.

items.q: A lift of mass $500\,\mathrm{kg}$ moves downwards with a constant acceleration of $2\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$ ($g=10\,\mathrm{N/kg}$). What is the tension in the cable?
items.explain: Down is positive: $mg-T=ma\Rightarrow T=m(g-a)=500(10-2)=4000\,\mathrm{N}$.

items.q: A man of mass $50\,\mathrm{kg}$ stands on a weighing scale in a lift that is descending with a constant DECELERATION of $1.0\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$ ($g=10\,\mathrm{N/kg}$). What does the scale read?
items.explain: Descending and slowing down means the acceleration is UPWARDS ($1.0\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$): $N-mg=ma\Rightarrow N=m(g+a)=50(11)=550\,\mathrm{N}$.

items.q: A man of mass $50\,\mathrm{kg}$ stands on a weighing scale in a lift that is descending with a constant ACCELERATION of $1.0\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$ ($g=10\,\mathrm{N/kg}$). What does the scale read?
items.explain: Accelerating downwards: $mg-N=ma\Rightarrow N=m(g-a)=50(9)=450\,\mathrm{N}$. He feels lighter.

items.q: A $1000\,\mathrm{kg}$ car is towed from rest until it reaches the towing vehicle's constant speed $0.8\,\mathrm{m/s}$. What is the change of momentum of the towed car?
items.explain: $\Delta p=m\Delta v=1000\times0.8=800\,\mathrm{kg\,m/s}$.

items.q: A $1000\,\mathrm{kg}$ car is towed from rest to $0.8\,\mathrm{m/s}$ by a rope with average tension $4000\,\mathrm{N}$. How far does the towed car travel while it speeds up?
items.explain:
Work-energy: $Fs=\tfrac12mv^2\Rightarrow s=\dfrac{\tfrac12(1000)(0.8)^2}{4000}=0.080\,\mathrm{m}$.
Check with impulse: $t=\Delta p/F=0.20\,\mathrm{s}$, $s=\bar vt=0.4\times0.2=0.080\,\mathrm{m}$.

items.q: In the same tow, the towing vehicle moves at a steady $0.8\,\mathrm{m/s}$ for the $0.20\,\mathrm{s}$ it takes the car to reach that speed. What is the minimum unstretched length of the rope if its breaking strain is $0.04$ (strain $=$ extension / original length)?
items.explain:
Towing vehicle: $0.8\times0.20=0.16\,\mathrm{m}$; towed car: $0.08\,\mathrm{m}$. The rope must stretch by $0.16-0.08=0.08\,\mathrm{m}$.
Strain $\le0.04\Rightarrow L\ge0.08/0.04=2.0\,\mathrm{m}$.

items.q: A block of mass $8.5\,\mathrm{kg}$ is held on a frictionless $30^\circ$ incline by a cord parallel to the slope. What is the tension in the cord?
items.explain: Along the slope the cord balances the weight component: $T=mg\sin\theta=8.5(9.8)\sin30^\circ=41.7\,\mathrm{N}$.

items.q: A block of mass $8.5\,\mathrm{kg}$ rests on a frictionless $30^\circ$ incline. What is the normal force on it?
items.explain: Perpendicular to the slope: $N=mg\cos\theta=8.5(9.8)\cos30^\circ=72.1\,\mathrm{N}$ (less than the weight $83.3\,\mathrm{N}$).

items.q: The cord holding the $8.5\,\mathrm{kg}$ block on the frictionless $30^\circ$ incline is cut. What is the magnitude of the block's acceleration?
items.explain: $a=g\sin\theta=9.8\sin30^\circ=4.9\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$, independent of the mass.

items.q: A block is projected up a frictionless $32.0^\circ$ incline with initial speed $3.50\,\mathrm{m/s}$. How far up the plane does it go?
items.explain:
Deceleration along the slope: $a=g\sin\theta=5.19\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$.
$d=\dfrac{v_0^2}{2a}=\dfrac{12.25}{10.39}=1.18\,\mathrm{m}$.

items.q: A block is projected up a frictionless $32.0^\circ$ incline at $3.50\,\mathrm{m/s}$. How long does it take to reach its highest point?
items.explain: $t=\dfrac{v_0}{g\sin\theta}=\dfrac{3.50}{5.19}=0.674\,\mathrm{s}$.

items.q: A block is projected up a frictionless incline at $3.50\,\mathrm{m/s}$. What is its speed when it returns to the bottom of the incline?
items.explain: Without friction mechanical energy is conserved: it returns to the same height with the same speed, $3.50\,\mathrm{m/s}$ (now directed down the slope).

items.q: A block $m_1=3.70\,\mathrm{kg}$ on a frictionless $30.0^\circ$ incline is connected by a cord over a frictionless pulley to a hanging block $m_2=2.30\,\mathrm{kg}$. What is the magnitude of the acceleration of the blocks?
items.explain:
Take down the slope and down for the hanging block as positive. Driving force: $m_2g-m_1g\sin\theta=22.54-18.13=4.41\,\mathrm{N}$.
$a=\dfrac{4.41}{6.00}=0.735\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$; the hanging block accelerates DOWNWARDS (it wins).

items.q: For the same arrangement ($m_1=3.70\,\mathrm{kg}$ on a $30.0^\circ$ frictionless slope, $m_2=2.30\,\mathrm{kg}$ hanging; $a=0.735\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$), what is the tension in the cord?
items.explain:
Hanging block: $m_2g-T=m_2a\Rightarrow T=m_2(g-a)=2.30(9.8-0.735)=20.8\,\mathrm{N}$.
Check with the block on the slope: $T-m_1g\sin\theta=m_1a\Rightarrow T=18.13+2.72=20.8\,\mathrm{N}$.

items.q: A certain force gives an object of mass $m_1$ an acceleration of $12.0\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$ and an object of mass $m_2$ an acceleration of $3.30\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$. What acceleration would the force give to an object of mass $m_2-m_1$?
With the same force (it gives $m_1$ an acceleration of $12.0\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$ and $m_2$ an acceleration of $3.30\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$), what acceleration does it give to an object of mass $m_2+m_1$?
items.explain: $\dfrac1a=\dfrac1{3.30}+\dfrac1{12.0}=0.386\Rightarrow a=2.59\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$.

items.q: A hockey puck is hit on a frozen lake and starts at $12\,\mathrm{m/s}$. Exactly $5.0\,\mathrm{s}$ later its speed is $6.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$. What is the coefficient of kinetic friction between the puck and the ice?
items.explain: Deceleration $=\dfrac{12-6}{5}=1.2\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$. The only horizontal force is friction: $\mu mg=ma\Rightarrow\mu=\dfrac{a}{g}=\dfrac{1.2}{9.8}=0.122$.

items.q: A hockey puck slows from $12\,\mathrm{m/s}$ to $6.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$ in $5.0\,\mathrm{s}$ on ice. How far does it travel in that time?
items.explain: Average speed $=\dfrac{12+6}{2}=9\,\mathrm{m/s}$, so $d=9.0\times5.0=45\,\mathrm{m}$.

items.q: A $3.00\,\mathrm{kg}$ block slides from rest down a $30.0^\circ$ incline, moving $2.00\,\mathrm{m}$ in $1.50\,\mathrm{s}$. What is its acceleration?
items.explain: From rest $s=\tfrac12at^2\Rightarrow a=\dfrac{2s}{t^2}=\dfrac{4.00}{2.25}=1.78\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$.

items.q: A $3.00\,\mathrm{kg}$ block slides down a $30.0^\circ$ incline with an acceleration of $1.78\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$. What is the coefficient of kinetic friction?
items.explain: Along the slope: $mg\sin\theta-\mu mg\cos\theta=ma\Rightarrow\mu=\dfrac{g\sin\theta-a}{g\cos\theta}=\dfrac{4.9-1.78}{8.49}=0.368$.

items.q: A $3.00\,\mathrm{kg}$ block slides down a $30.0^\circ$ incline with $\mu_k=0.368$. What is the magnitude of the friction force on it?
items.explain: $f=\mu_kN=\mu_k\,mg\cos\theta=0.368(3.00)(9.8)\cos30^\circ=9.37\,\mathrm{N}$.

items.q: A $3.00\,\mathrm{kg}$ block starts from rest and accelerates down a $30.0^\circ$ incline at $1.78\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$. What is its speed after sliding $2.00\,\mathrm{m}$?
items.explain: $v^2=2as=2(1.78)(2.00)\Rightarrow v=2.67\,\mathrm{m/s}$ (or $v=at=1.78\times1.50=2.67\,\mathrm{m/s}$).

items.q: Blocks A and B weigh $44\,\mathrm{N}$ and $22\,\mathrm{N}$. A lies on a table and is tied over a frictionless pulley to the hanging block B. Block C rests on A. What is the minimum weight of C that keeps A from sliding if $\mu_s=0.2$ between A and the table?
items.explain:
Static friction must balance the tension $T=W_B=22\,\mathrm{N}$: $\mu_s(W_A+W_C)\ge22\Rightarrow W_A+W_C\ge110\,\mathrm{N}$.
$W_C\ge110-44=66\,\mathrm{N}$.

items.q: Blocks A (weight $44\,\mathrm{N}$, on a table with $\mu_k=0.15$) and B (weight $22\,\mathrm{N}$, hanging) are joined over a frictionless pulley. Block C is lifted off A. What is the acceleration of A?
items.explain:
Driving force $W_B-\mu_kW_A=22-6.6=15.4\,\mathrm{N}$ on the total mass $(44+22)/9.8=6.73\,\mathrm{kg}$.
$a=\dfrac{15.4}{6.73}=2.29\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$.

items.q: A $5\,\mathrm{kg}$ crate is pulled along a horizontal floor by a horizontal force of $30\,\mathrm{N}$. The coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.2. What is the acceleration of the crate?
items.explain:
Friction $f=\mu mg=0.2(5)(9.8)=9.8\,\mathrm{N}$.
$a=\dfrac{F-f}{m}=\dfrac{30-9.8}{5}=4.04\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$.

items.q: What is the difference between mass and weight?
opts: Mass is the amount of matter and does not depend on location; weight $=mg$ is a force that depends on $g$
Mass depends on location; weight does not
They are the same quantity measured in different units
Mass is a force; weight is the amount of matter
items.explain: Mass (kg) is an intrinsic property; weight (N) is the gravitational force $W=mg$, which would be about six times smaller on the Moon.

items.q: A $10\,\mathrm{kg}$ block rests on a horizontal table and a hand pushes it vertically DOWN with $20\,\mathrm{N}$. The normal force from the table is
items.explain: Vertical equilibrium: $N=mg+F=98+20=118\,\mathrm{N}$. The normal force adjusts to whatever is needed; it is not always equal to the weight.

items.q: Which statement about the maximum static friction $f_{s,\max}$ and kinetic friction $f_k$ between the same two surfaces is correct?
opts: Both depend on the contact area
Both are independent of the normal force
items.explain: $f_{s,\max}=\mu_sN$ and $f_k=\mu_kN$ with $\mu_s\ge\mu_k$ in general; both are proportional to the normal force and (in this model) independent of the contact area.

items.q: A free-body diagram of a block sliding down a rough incline must show
opts: weight, normal force and friction (up the slope)
weight, normal force and a 'force of motion' down the slope
weight, normal force, and friction pointing down the slope
items.explain: Include only real forces: gravity, the contact normal force and kinetic friction opposing the sliding. There is no separate 'force of motion'.

items.q: A force of $12\,\mathrm{N}$ and a force of $5\,\mathrm{N}$ act on a body at right angles to each other. The magnitude of the resultant is
items.explain: Perpendicular forces: $F=\sqrt{12^2+5^2}=13\,\mathrm{N}$ (not $12+5$).

items.q: A net force of $24\,\mathrm{N}$ acts on a $6.0\,\mathrm{kg}$ body initially at rest. What is its speed after $3.0\,\mathrm{s}$?
items.explain: $a=F/m=4.0\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$; $v=at=12\,\mathrm{m/s}$.

items.q: Which statement correctly describes the principle of conservation of momentum?
opts: Momentum is conserved only in elastic collisions
Momentum is the product of mass and velocity
Momentum is conserved by every body in a collision
Momentum of a system is conserved provided no external force acts on it
items.explain:
For an isolated system the total momentum is constant in ALL collisions (elastic or not). The individual bodies exchange momentum, so a single body does not conserve its own.
Option 4 defines momentum; it does not state the principle.

items.q: In a collision between two steel balls suspended on strings (a nearly elastic collision), which quantities are conserved?
opts: kinetic energy and total energy only
kinetic energy, total energy and momentum
items.explain: Elastic collision: momentum, kinetic energy and (as always) total energy are conserved. In an inelastic collision kinetic energy would be partly converted to heat or deformation.

items.q: Two spheres of equal mass $m$ move towards each other with speed $v$ and collide head-on elastically. Which statement is correct?
opts: The total kinetic energy before impact is zero
The total momentum before impact is $2mv$
The total kinetic energy after impact is $mv^2$
items.explain: Total momentum before $=mv-mv=0$ (so option 4 is wrong). Total kinetic energy before $=2\cdot\tfrac12mv^2=mv^2$, and the collision is elastic, so it is $mv^2$ afterwards too (the spheres simply reverse).

items.q: A body initially at rest explodes into two parts of masses $M_1$ and $M_2$ that move apart with speeds $v_1$ and $v_2$. What is $v_1/v_2$?
items.explain: Initial momentum zero: $M_1v_1=M_2v_2\Rightarrow\dfrac{v_1}{v_2}=\dfrac{M_2}{M_1}$. The lighter piece moves faster.

items.q: A particle of mass $m$ and velocity $u$ collides head-on and elastically with a stationary particle of mass $M$. What is the velocity of $M$ afterwards?
items.explain:
Momentum: $mu=mv_1+Mv_2$. Elastic: $u=v_2-v_1$ (relative speed of approach = relative speed of separation).
Eliminating $v_1$: $v_2=\dfrac{2mu}{M+m}$. The expression $\dfrac{(M-m)u}{M+m}$ is $-v_1$ in magnitude, the velocity of the incoming particle.

items.q: A 2 kg cart moving at 8 m/s collides head-on and elastically with a stationary 6 kg cart. What is the velocity of the second cart after the collision?
items.explain:
$v_2=\dfrac{2m u}{m+M}=\dfrac{2(2)(8)}{8}=4\,\mathrm{m/s}$.
First cart: $v_1=\dfrac{m-M}{m+M}u=-4\,\mathrm{m/s}$; momentum and kinetic energy are both conserved.
items.src: Generated, same style as: Mechanics tutorial Part 4, Q2

items.q: A 1.5 kg cart moving at 4 m/s collides head-on and elastically with a stationary 1.5 kg cart. What is the velocity of the second cart after the collision?
items.explain:
$v_2=\dfrac{2m u}{m+M}=\dfrac{2(1.5)(4)}{3}=4\,\mathrm{m/s}$.
First cart: $v_1=\dfrac{m-M}{m+M}u=0\,\mathrm{m/s}$; momentum and kinetic energy are both conserved.

items.q: A 3 kg cart moving at 6 m/s collides head-on and elastically with a stationary 1 kg cart. What is the velocity of the second cart after the collision?
items.explain:
$v_2=\dfrac{2m u}{m+M}=\dfrac{2(3)(6)}{4}=9\,\mathrm{m/s}$.
First cart: $v_1=\dfrac{m-M}{m+M}u=3\,\mathrm{m/s}$; momentum and kinetic energy are both conserved.

items.q: A sphere of mass $m$ on a string of length $\ell$ is released from the horizontal position and strikes, at the bottom, a block of mass $4m$ at rest on a smooth table (perfectly elastic collision). The velocity of the block just after the collision is
opts: $\dfrac25\sqrt{2g\ell}$ in the direction of the sphere's motion
$\dfrac35\sqrt{2g\ell}$ in the direction of the sphere's motion
$\sqrt{2g\ell}$ in the direction of the sphere's motion
items.explain:
Swing: $mg\ell=\tfrac12mv^2\Rightarrow v=\sqrt{2g\ell}$.
Elastic collision with $M=4m$: $v_M=\dfrac{2m}{m+4m}v=\dfrac25\sqrt{2g\ell}$ and the sphere rebounds with $\dfrac{m-4m}{5m}v=-\dfrac35\sqrt{2g\ell}$.
Check: momentum $m v=m(-\tfrac35v)+4m(\tfrac25v)=m v$.

items.q: A $2150\,\mathrm{kg}$ car moving east at $10.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$ collides with a $3250\,\mathrm{kg}$ car also moving east. The cars stick together and move at $5.22\,\mathrm{m/s}$. What was the velocity of the $3250\,\mathrm{kg}$ car before the collision?

The cars of the previous problem ($2150\,\mathrm{kg}$ at $10.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$ and $3250\,\mathrm{kg}$ at $2.06\,\mathrm{m/s}$) stick together and move off at $5.22\,\mathrm{m/s}$. How much kinetic energy is lost?
items.explain:
Before: $\tfrac12(2150)(10.0)^2+\tfrac12(3250)(2.058)^2=1.075\times10^5+6.88\times10^3=1.144\times10^5\,\mathrm{J}$.
After: $\tfrac12(5400)(5.22)^2=7.36\times10^4\,\mathrm{J}$.
Loss $\approx4.1\times10^4\,\mathrm{J}$. Check with $\Delta K=\dfrac{m_1m_2}{2(m_1+m_2)}(v_1-v_2)^2=4.1\times10^4\,\mathrm{J}$.

items.q: An unstable nucleus of mass $17.0\times10^{-27}\,\mathrm{kg}$ at rest disintegrates into three particles. One ($5.0\times10^{-27}\,\mathrm{kg}$) moves along $+y$ at $6.0\times10^{6}\,\mathrm{m/s}$; another ($8.4\times10^{-27}\,\mathrm{kg}$) moves along $+x$ at $4.0\times10^{6}\,\mathrm{m/s}$. What is the speed of the third particle?
items.explain:
Third mass: $17.0-5.0-8.4=3.6\times10^{-27}\,\mathrm{kg}$.
Momentum components of the third particle: $p_x=-(8.4\times10^{-27})(4.0\times10^6)=-3.36\times10^{-20}$, $p_y=-(5.0\times10^{-27})(6.0\times10^6)=-3.0\times10^{-20}\,\mathrm{kg\,m/s}$.
$|p|=4.50\times10^{-20}$, so $v=\dfrac{4.50\times10^{-20}}{3.6\times10^{-27}}=1.25\times10^{7}\,\mathrm{m/s}$, at $222^\circ$ from $+x$ (third quadrant).

items.q: A $12\,\mathrm{g}$ bullet strikes a stationary $5.2\,\mathrm{kg}$ wooden block on a frictionless surface and embeds in it; block plus bullet move at $1.7\,\mathrm{m/s}$. What was the speed of the bullet?
items.explain: $mv_b=(m+M)v\Rightarrow v_b=\dfrac{(0.012+5.2)(1.7)}{0.012}=7.4\times10^2\,\mathrm{m/s}$. Convert $12\,\mathrm{g}=0.012\,\mathrm{kg}$.

items.q: A bullet embeds in a block (bullet $12\,\mathrm{g}$, block $5.2\,\mathrm{kg}$). What fraction of the bullet's initial kinetic energy is dissipated?
items.explain: Fraction lost $=1-\dfrac{\tfrac12(m+M)v^2}{\tfrac12mv_b^2}=\dfrac{M}{m+M}=0.9977$: practically all of it.

items.q: A $5\,\mathrm{kg}$ object moving at $4.5\,\mathrm{m/s}$ hits a $2.5\,\mathrm{kg}$ object at rest on a frictionless surface. Afterwards both move at $30^\circ$ on either side of the original line. What is the final speed of the $5\,\mathrm{kg}$ object?
items.explain:
$y$-momentum: $m_1v_1\sin30^\circ=m_2v_2\sin30^\circ\Rightarrow v_2=2v_1$.
$x$-momentum: $m_1u_1=(m_1v_1+m_2v_2)\cos30^\circ=10v_1\cos30^\circ\Rightarrow v_1=\dfrac{22.5}{8.66}=2.60\,\mathrm{m/s}$, $v_2=5.20\,\mathrm{m/s}$.

items.q: For the same collision (5 kg at 4.5 m/s hits 2.5 kg at rest; final speeds $2.60$ and $5.20\,\mathrm{m/s}$ at $30^\circ$ either side), is the collision elastic?
opts: No: momentum is not conserved in two dimensions
Yes: the total kinetic energy is $50.6\,\mathrm{J}$ before and after
No: about half of the kinetic energy is lost
Cannot be decided without the masses of the surfaces
items.explain: Before: $\tfrac12(5)(4.5)^2=50.6\,\mathrm{J}$. After: $\tfrac12(5)(2.60)^2+\tfrac12(2.5)(5.20)^2=16.9+33.8=50.6\,\mathrm{J}$ - equal, so the collision is elastic.

items.q: A $0.35\,\mathrm{kg}$ softball pitched at $12\,\mathrm{m/s}$ is hit straight back at $21\,\mathrm{m/s}$. What impulse does the bat give the ball?
items.explain: Take the batted direction as positive: $J=\Delta p=m(v_f-v_i)=0.35[21-(-12)]=11.6\,\mathrm{N\,s}$. The velocity REVERSES, so the speeds add.

items.q: The bat in the previous problem acts on the ball for $0.01\,\mathrm{s}$ and gives it an impulse of $11.55\,\mathrm{N\,s}$. What is the average force?
items.explain: $\bar F=\dfrac{J}{\Delta t}=\dfrac{11.55}{0.01}=1.16\times10^3\,\mathrm{N}$ (about $330$ times the weight of the ball).

items.q: What is the main energy change while a light bulb operates?
opts: heat and light to electrical energy
electrical energy to heat and light
items.explain: A lamp transforms electrical energy into light and (mostly) heat.

items.q: What are the main energy changes in a battery-operated remote-control car?
items.explain: The battery stores chemical energy, which becomes electrical energy in the circuit, which the motor turns into kinetic energy (plus some heat).

items.q: A battery supplies $500\,\mathrm{J}$ of electrical energy to a motor which moves an object $40\,\mathrm{m}$ horizontally under a $6\,\mathrm{N}$ pulling force. What is the efficiency of the motor (as a percentage)?
items.explain:
Useful work $=Fd=6\times40=240\,\mathrm{J}$.
Efficiency $=\dfrac{240}{500}=0.48=48\%$.

items.q: A particle is displaced from $\vec r_1=(3\hat i+2\hat j-6\hat k)\,\mathrm{m}$ to $\vec r_2=(14\hat i+13\hat j+9\hat k)\,\mathrm{m}$ by a force $5\hat i\,\mathrm{N}$. How much work does the force do?
items.explain: $W=\vec F\cdot\Delta\vec r$ with $\Delta\vec r=(11,11,15)\,\mathrm{m}$: only the $x$-component counts, $W=5\times11=55\,\mathrm{J}$.

items.q: A force $F$ acting on an object varies with position as shown. How much work does it do between $x=0$ and $x=6\,\mathrm{m}$?
items.explain: Work $=$ area under the $F$-$x$ graph $=\tfrac12(2)(3)+(2)(3)+\tfrac12(2)(3)=3+6+3=12\,\mathrm{J}$.

items.q: A cord, pulled over a pulley $h=1.20\,\mathrm{m}$ above the cart's level, drags a cart along a frictionless rail from $x_1=3.00\,\mathrm{m}$ to $x_2=1.00\,\mathrm{m}$. The cord tension is a constant $25.0\,\mathrm{N}$. What is the change in the kinetic energy of the cart?
items.explain:
Work by the tension $=T\times$ (decrease in the length of cord from the pulley to the cart).
Length: $\sqrt{x_1^2+h^2}=\sqrt{10.44}=3.231\,\mathrm{m}$ and $\sqrt{x_2^2+h^2}=\sqrt{2.44}=1.562\,\mathrm{m}$.
$\Delta K=25.0(3.231-1.562)=41.7\,\mathrm{J}$. Using $T\Delta x=50\,\mathrm{J}$ would ignore that the force is not horizontal.

items.q: A ball is thrown off a cliff with the same initial speed $v_0$ (A) upward, (B) horizontally, (C) downward. If air resistance is negligible, how do the speeds on reaching the ground compare?
items.explain: Gravity is conservative: the speed at the ground depends only on the starting speed and the height drop, $v=\sqrt{v_0^2+2gh}$ - the same for every direction of launch.

items.q: A ball of mass $m$ swings from height $h$ and collides elastically, at the lowest point, with a block of mass $2m$ at rest on a frictionless surface. To what height does the ball rise afterwards?
items.explain: Speed at the bottom $v=\sqrt{2gh}$. Elastic collision: $v_{\text{ball}}=\dfrac{m-2m}{3m}v=-\dfrac v3$. Its kinetic energy is $\dfrac19$ of the original, so it rises to $h/9$.

items.q: A block of mass $m$ slides down an incline at constant speed from height $h$ (coefficient of kinetic friction $\mu$). How much energy is dissipated by friction by the time it reaches the bottom?
items.explain: Constant speed means $\Delta K=0$: all the gravitational potential energy lost, $mgh$, is converted to thermal energy (equivalently $f\cdot L=mg\sin\theta\,(h/\sin\theta)=mgh$).

items.q: A $3\,\mathrm{kg}$ block starts from rest at height $43\,\mathrm{cm}$ on a $35^\circ$ incline, slides down, and then along a horizontal surface. The coefficient of kinetic friction is $0.25$ on both surfaces. How far does it slide on the horizontal surface before stopping?
items.explain:
Work-kinetic energy theorem over the whole path: $mgh-\mu mg\cos\theta\,\dfrac{h}{\sin\theta}-\mu mg\,d=0$.
$d=\dfrac h\mu-\dfrac{h}{\tan\theta}=1.72-0.614=1.11\,\mathrm{m}$. (The mass cancels.)

items.q: A $25\,\mathrm{kg}$ child on a $2.0\,\mathrm{m}$ long swing is released from rest with the supports at $30^\circ$ to the vertical. What is the child's maximum gravitational potential energy (zero at the lowest point)?
items.explain:
Height above the lowest point: $h=L(1-\cos30^\circ)=2.0(0.134)=0.268\,\mathrm{m}$.
$U=mgh=25(9.8)(0.2679)=65.6\,\mathrm{J}$.

items.q: The same swing: what is the child's speed at the lowest position if friction is disregarded?
items.explain: Energy conservation: $\tfrac12mv^2=mgh\Rightarrow v=\sqrt{2gh}=\sqrt{2(9.8)(0.268)}=2.29\,\mathrm{m/s}$.

items.q: The swing child ($25\,\mathrm{kg}$, released from a height $0.268\,\mathrm{m}$ above the lowest point) actually has speed $2.00\,\mathrm{m/s}$ at the lowest position. What is the change in mechanical energy due to friction?
items.explain:
Final mechanical energy $=\tfrac12(25)(2.00)^2=50.0\,\mathrm{J}$; initial $=65.6\,\mathrm{J}$.
$\Delta E=50.0-65.6=-15.6\,\mathrm{J}$ (15.6 J lost as heat).

items.q: A pirate drags a $50\,\mathrm{kg}$ chest $6\,\mathrm{m}$ along a dock with a constant $95\,\mathrm{N}$ force $15^\circ$ above the horizontal. How much work does the pirate do?
items.explain: $W=Fd\cos\theta=95(6)\cos15^\circ=551\,\mathrm{J}$.

items.q: The pirate pulls the $50\,\mathrm{kg}$ chest at $15^\circ$ above the horizontal with $95\,\mathrm{N}$ ($\mu_k=0.15$, distance $6\,\mathrm{m}$). How much energy is dissipated as heat by friction?
items.explain:
The upward component of the pull reduces the normal force: $N=mg-F\sin15^\circ=490-24.6=465\,\mathrm{N}$.
$Q=\mu Nd=0.15(465)(6)=419\,\mathrm{J}$. (Using $N=mg$ would give $441\,\mathrm{J}$.)

items.q: The pirate's chest ($50\,\mathrm{kg}$) receives $551\,\mathrm{J}$ of work from the pull and loses $419\,\mathrm{J}$ to friction. What is its final speed (starting from rest)?
items.explain: Work-energy theorem: $\tfrac12mv^2=W_{\text{net}}=551-419=132\,\mathrm{J}$, so $v=\sqrt{\dfrac{2(132)}{50}}=2.3\,\mathrm{m/s}$.

items.q: Starting from rest, a $10.0\,\mathrm{kg}$ suitcase slides $3.00\,\mathrm{m}$ down a frictionless ramp inclined at $30.0^\circ$. What is its speed at the bottom?
items.explain: Height drop $=3.00\sin30^\circ=1.50\,\mathrm{m}$; $\tfrac12mv^2=mgh\Rightarrow v=\sqrt{2(9.8)(1.50)}=5.42\,\mathrm{m/s}$.

items.q: The suitcase then slides a further $5.00\,\mathrm{m}$ along the floor before stopping. What is the coefficient of kinetic friction on the floor?
items.explain: $\tfrac12mv^2=\mu mgd\Rightarrow\mu=\dfrac{v^2}{2gd}=\dfrac{29.4}{2(9.8)(5.00)}=0.300$. Equivalently all the potential energy $mg(1.5)$ is dissipated over $5.00\,\mathrm{m}$: $\mu=1.5/5.0$.

items.q: Using the same suitcase ($10.0\,\mathrm{kg}$, speed $5.42\,\mathrm{m/s}$ at the bottom of the ramp, then stopped on the floor), what is the change in mechanical energy due to friction on the floor?
items.explain: The suitcase loses all of its kinetic energy: $\Delta E=0-\tfrac12(10.0)(5.42)^2=-147\,\mathrm{J}$.

items.q: A block $m_1$ on a horizontal surface is joined to a spring of constant $k$ and, over a frictionless pulley, to a hanging block $m_2$. Released from rest with the spring unstretched, $m_2$ falls a distance $h$ before momentarily stopping. The coefficient of kinetic friction of $m_1$ is
items.explain:
Energy: lost potential energy of $m_2$ = spring energy + heat: $m_2gh=\tfrac12kh^2+\mu m_1gh$.
$\mu=\dfrac{m_2g-\tfrac12kh}{m_1g}$. The spring force is not constant, so its work is $\tfrac12kh^2$, not $kh\cdot h$.

items.q: Which word equation correctly defines power?
opts: force $\times$ distance moved in the direction of the force
items.explain: Power is the rate of doing work, $P=W/t$. Option 1 is the work; option 2 is a formula that equals the power for a force along the velocity.

items.q: A body of mass $m$ is moved a distance $s$ at a steady speed $v$ against a constant force $F$. What power is required?
items.explain: $P=\dfrac{Fs}{t}=Fv$.

items.q: A car engine provides $24\,\mathrm{kW}$ of useful power to travel at constant speed. The driving force is $600\,\mathrm{N}$. What is the speed of the car?
items.explain: $P=Fv\Rightarrow v=\dfrac{P}{F}=\dfrac{24000}{600}=40\,\mathrm{m/s}$.

items.q: A crane lifts its hook (steady force $1000\,\mathrm{N}$) together with a $1000\,\mathrm{kg}$ load at $0.5\,\mathrm{m/s}$ ($g=10\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$). What power is used?
items.explain:
Total lifting force at constant velocity $=1000+1000(10)=11000\,\mathrm{N}$.
$P=Fv=11000\times0.5=5500\,\mathrm{W}=5.5\,\mathrm{kW}$.

items.q: A body of mass $m$ moves up a frictionless track inclined at $\theta$ to the horizontal. What power is needed to give it a forward acceleration $a$ when its velocity is $v$?
items.explain: Force along the track: $F=ma+mg\sin\theta$. Power $=Fv=mav+mgv\sin\theta$.

items.q: A force of 30 N pulls a 4 kg sled 5 m along level ice at 40° above the horizontal. How much work does the force do?
items.explain: $W=Fd\cos\theta=30\times5\times\cos40^\circ=115\,\mathrm{J}$. Only the component of the force along the displacement does work.

Do not square the difference of the speeds: $(v_2-v_1)^2\ne v_2^2-v_1^2$.

Collision (momentum): $mv_b=(m+M)v\Rightarrow v_b=\dfrac{1.52}{0.020}(1.53)=1.2\times10^2\,\mathrm{m/s}$.

items.q: A force acts on an object that moves in a circle at constant speed, always along the radius towards the centre. How much work does this centripetal force do in one revolution?
items.explain: The force is perpendicular to the displacement at each instant ($\cos90^\circ=0$), so it does no work; the speed does not change.

items.q: Which of the following forces is NOT conservative?
items.explain: The work of a conservative force depends only on the end points. Friction's work depends on the path length, so it is non-conservative (it dissipates mechanical energy).

items.q: In a perfectly inelastic collision between two bodies,
opts: momentum is conserved and the maximum possible kinetic energy is lost
both momentum and kinetic energy are lost
the bodies bounce apart with the same total kinetic energy
kinetic energy is conserved but momentum is not
items.explain: The bodies stick together and move with the velocity of the centre of mass. Momentum is conserved; the kinetic energy that is lost is the largest possible while still conserving momentum.

items.q: A particle moves along a circular arc of length $\ell$ and radius $r$ in time $t$. Which expression gives its angular velocity about the centre?
items.explain: Angle swept $\theta=\ell/r$, so $\omega=\dfrac\theta t=\dfrac{\ell}{rt}$ (check: the linear speed $\ell/t=\omega r$).

items.q: Particles P and Q are on a rotating circular plate; the distance of P from the axis is twice that of Q. What is (linear velocity of P) / (linear velocity of Q)?
items.explain: Same $\omega$ for every point of a rigid plate; $v=\omega r$, so $v_P/v_Q=r_P/r_Q=2$.

items.q: A communication satellite moves at constant speed in a circular orbit around the Earth. Which row is correct for its momentum and kinetic energy?
items.explain: Momentum $m\vec v$ is a vector: its direction keeps changing, so it is not constant. Kinetic energy $\tfrac12mv^2$ depends only on the (constant) speed.

items.q: Which statement is correct for a particle in a horizontal circle with constant angular velocity?
opts: Both kinetic energy and linear momentum are constant
Both speed and linear velocity are constant
The kinetic energy is constant but the linear momentum varies
The linear momentum is constant but the kinetic energy varies
items.explain: Speed (hence $K$) is constant; the velocity vector and momentum change direction.

items.q: A body in uniform circular motion has the following behaviour of linear velocity, angular velocity and linear acceleration:
items.explain: Velocity is a vector whose direction rotates (varying); $\omega$ is constant; the centripetal acceleration has constant magnitude but its direction rotates, so the acceleration vector varies.

items.q: What is the mean angular speed of the minute hand of a clock?
items.explain: One revolution ($2\pi\,\mathrm{rad}$) per $3600\,\mathrm{s}$: $\omega=\dfrac{2\pi}{3600}=1.7\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{rad/s}$.

items.q: A spacecraft moves in a circular orbit when its engine fires, producing a force exactly equal and opposite to Earth's gravitational pull. How does the spacecraft move afterwards?
opts: radially along the line to the Earth's centre
in a circular orbit with a longer period
along a spiral path towards the Earth
along a tangent to the orbit
items.explain: Net force becomes zero, so Newton's first law applies: it continues in a straight line with its velocity at that instant, tangent to the circle.

items.q: An engine component rotates at $3000$ revolutions per minute in a circle of radius $8.0\,\mathrm{cm}$. What is its centripetal acceleration?
items.explain:
$\omega=3000\times\dfrac{2\pi}{60}=314\,\mathrm{rad/s}$.
$a_c=\omega^2r=(314)^2(0.080)=7.9\times10^{3}\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$ (convert $8.0\,\mathrm{cm}$ to $0.080\,\mathrm{m}$).

items.q: A pendulum bob of mass $1.27\,\mathrm{kg}$ hangs from a string of length $0.600\,\mathrm{m}$. When the string is vertical the bob moves horizontally at $0.575\,\mathrm{m/s}$. What is the tension in the string? ($g=9.81\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$)
items.explain:
At the lowest point the net force is centripetal (upwards): $T-mg=\dfrac{mv^2}{L}$.
$T=mg+\dfrac{mv^2}{L}=12.46+0.70=13.2\,\mathrm{N}$.

items.q: A pendulum bob of mass $m$ and weight $W$ swings on a string of length $r$. When the string is vertical the tension is $T$ and the speed is $v$. Which relation is correct?
items.explain: Net force towards the centre (upwards) is $T-W=\dfrac{mv^2}{r}$. Option 2 has the wrong dimensions (missing the mass).

items.q: A car of mass $m$ travels at constant speed $v$ over a humpback bridge of radius $r$ and stays in contact with the road. The force it exerts on the road at the top is
items.explain: Centre of curvature is below: $mg-N=\dfrac{mv^2}{r}\Rightarrow N=mg-\dfrac{mv^2}{r}$, and the car pushes on the road with the same force $R$ (third law). The car loses contact when $v=\sqrt{gr}$.

items.q: A body is released from rest at height $h$ on a frictionless incline that leads into a vertical loop of radius $R$. What is the minimum $h$ for the body to complete the loop?
items.explain:
At the top of the loop the normal force can be zero at best: $mg=\dfrac{mv^2}{R}\Rightarrow v^2=gR$.
Energy from the release point to the top: $mgh=mg(2R)+\tfrac12mv^2=2mgR+\tfrac12mgR$, so $h=2.5R$.

items.q: A $25.0\,\mathrm{kg}$ sled on frictionless ice is tied by a $5.00\,\mathrm{m}$ rope to a post and revolves uniformly, making five complete revolutions every minute. What force does the rope exert on it?
items.explain:
$\omega=\dfrac{5(2\pi)}{60}=0.524\,\mathrm{rad/s}$.
Rope tension supplies the centripetal force: $F=m\omega^2r=25.0(0.524)^2(5.00)=34.3\,\mathrm{N}$.

items.q: A car rounds a flat unbanked curve of radius $50.0\,\mathrm{m}$. The coefficient of static friction between tyres and road is $0.70$. What is the maximum speed without sliding?
items.explain: Friction supplies the centripetal force: $\mu mg\ge\dfrac{mv^2}{R}\Rightarrow v_{\max}=\sqrt{\mu gR}=\sqrt{0.70(9.8)(50.0)}=18.5\,\mathrm{m/s}$ ($\approx67\,\mathrm{km/h}$).

items.q: A stone on a string moves in a horizontal circle of radius 0.5 m with a period of 2 s. What is its centripetal acceleration?
items.explain:
$a_c=\dfrac{4\pi^2r}{T^2}=\dfrac{4\pi^2(0.5)}{2^2}=4.93\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$.
Second route: $v=2\pi r/T=1.57\,\mathrm{m/s}$ and $a_c=v^2/r$ gives the same value.

items.q: A stone on a string moves in a horizontal circle of radius 0.1 m with a period of 0.25 s. What is its centripetal acceleration?
items.explain:
$a_c=\dfrac{4\pi^2r}{T^2}=\dfrac{4\pi^2(0.1)}{0.25^2}=63.2\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$.
Second route: $v=2\pi r/T=2.51\,\mathrm{m/s}$ and $a_c=v^2/r$ gives the same value.

items.q: A 0.8 kg object whirled on a string in a VERTICAL circle of radius 1.2 m has speed 5 m/s at the lowest point. What is the tension there?
items.explain:
Lowest point, centre above: $T-mg=\dfrac{mv^2}{r}\Rightarrow T=m\left(g+\dfrac{v^2}{r}\right)=24.5\,\mathrm{N}$.
At the lowest point the tension is the largest; the weight adds to the centripetal requirement.

items.q: A 2 kg object whirled on a string in a VERTICAL circle of radius 0.6 m has speed 3 m/s at the lowest point. What is the tension there?
items.explain:
Lowest point, centre above: $T-mg=\dfrac{mv^2}{r}\Rightarrow T=m\left(g+\dfrac{v^2}{r}\right)=49.6\,\mathrm{N}$.
At the lowest point the tension is the largest; the weight adds to the centripetal requirement.

items.q: What is the minimum speed at the TOP of a vertical circle of radius 0.8 m for an object on a string to keep the string taut?
items.explain:
At the minimum speed the tension vanishes: $mg=\dfrac{mv^2}{R}\Rightarrow v=\sqrt{gR}=2.8\,\mathrm{m/s}$.
The matching minimum speed at the bottom is $\sqrt{5gR}$ (energy conservation).

items.q: What is the minimum speed at the TOP of a vertical circle of radius 2 m for an object on a string to keep the string taut?
items.explain:
At the minimum speed the tension vanishes: $mg=\dfrac{mv^2}{R}\Rightarrow v=\sqrt{gR}=4.43\,\mathrm{m/s}$.
The matching minimum speed at the bottom is $\sqrt{5gR}$ (energy conservation).

items.q: A frictionless banked curve of radius $100\,\mathrm{m}$ is designed for $20\,\mathrm{m/s}$. What is the banking angle?
items.explain:
Only the horizontal component of the normal force supplies the centripetal force: $N\sin\theta=\dfrac{mv^2}{R}$, $N\cos\theta=mg$.
$\tan\theta=\dfrac{v^2}{gR}=\dfrac{400}{980}=0.408\Rightarrow\theta=22.2^\circ$.

items.q: A wheel starting at angular speed 0 rad/s has a constant angular acceleration of 2 rad/s². What is its angular speed after 5 s?
items.explain: $\omega=\omega_0+\alpha t=0+2\times5=10\,\mathrm{rad/s}$.
items.src: Generated, same style as: Lecture 5 (rotation with constant angular acceleration)

items.q: A wheel starting at 0 rad/s has constant angular acceleration 2 rad/s². Through what angle does it turn in 5 s?
items.explain: $\theta=\omega_0t+\tfrac12\alpha t^2=25\,\mathrm{rad}$. Check: $\omega^2=\omega_0^2+2\alpha\theta$ gives the same angle.

items.q: A wheel starting at angular speed 4 rad/s has a constant angular acceleration of 3 rad/s². What is its angular speed after 6 s?
items.explain: $\omega=\omega_0+\alpha t=4+3\times6=22\,\mathrm{rad/s}$.

items.q: A wheel starting at 4 rad/s has constant angular acceleration 3 rad/s². Through what angle does it turn in 6 s?

items.q: A point on a rotating disk is $0.25\,\mathrm{m}$ from the axis. At an instant the disk has $\omega=8.0\,\mathrm{rad/s}$ and $\alpha=3.0\,\mathrm{rad/s^2}$. What is the magnitude of the point's total linear acceleration?
items.explain:
Tangential: $a_t=\alpha r=0.75\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$. Radial (centripetal): $a_r=\omega^2r=16.0\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$.
They are perpendicular: $a=\sqrt{0.75^2+16.0^2}=16.0\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$.

items.q: A flywheel turns at $1200$ revolutions per minute. Express its angular speed in rad/s.
items.explain: $\omega=1200\times\dfrac{2\pi\,\mathrm{rad}}{60\,\mathrm{s}}=126\,\mathrm{rad/s}$.

items.q: A wheel of radius $0.30\,\mathrm{m}$ rolls without slipping at $6.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$. Through how many revolutions does it turn in $10\,\mathrm{s}$?
items.explain:
Distance rolled $=60\,\mathrm{m}$; one revolution covers the circumference $2\pi(0.30)=1.885\,\mathrm{m}$.
Revolutions $=\dfrac{60}{1.885}=31.8$.

items.q: The SI unit of angular velocity is
items.explain: $\omega=\Delta\theta/\Delta t$ in radians per second (rev/min is a common non-SI unit).

items.q: In uniform circular motion the centripetal acceleration is directed
opts: towards the centre of the circle
items.explain: The acceleration changes the direction, not the magnitude, of the velocity, so it is perpendicular to $\vec v$ and points inward: $a_c=v^2/r$.

items.q: A coin rests on a turntable that spins faster and faster. The coin finally slides off. Which force provides the coin's centripetal force until then?
items.explain: Static friction acting towards the centre; it can only supply $\mu_smg$, so the coin slips when $m\omega^2r>\mu_smg$. 'Centrifugal force' is not a real force in an inertial frame.

items.q: A $0.50\,\mathrm{kg}$ ball on a $1.0\,\mathrm{m}$ string moves in a horizontal circle at $4.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$ on a frictionless table. What is the tension?
items.src: Generated, same style as: Mechanics tutorial Part 5, Q9

items.q: A rider of mass $60\,\mathrm{kg}$ sits on a Ferris wheel of radius $12\,\mathrm{m}$ that makes one revolution every $20\,\mathrm{s}$. What is the normal force of the seat on the rider at the TOP of the ride?
items.explain:
Speed $v=\dfrac{2\pi R}{T}=3.77\,\mathrm{m/s}$, so $a_c=\dfrac{v^2}{R}=1.18\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$ (towards the centre, i.e. downwards at the top).
$mg-N=ma_c\Rightarrow N=m(g-a_c)=60(9.8-1.18)=517\,\mathrm{N}$: the rider feels lighter at the top (and heavier, $659\,\mathrm{N}$, at the bottom).
items.src: Generated, same style as: Mechanics tutorial Part 5, Q11

items.q: The same rider ($60\,\mathrm{kg}$) on a Ferris wheel of radius $12\,\mathrm{m}$ with period $20\,\mathrm{s}$: what does the seat push with at the BOTTOM of the ride?
items.explain: At the bottom the centre is above: $N-mg=ma_c\Rightarrow N=m(g+a_c)=60(9.8+1.18)=659\,\mathrm{N}$.
items.src: Generated, same style as: Mechanics tutorial Part 5, Q9

items.q: A conical pendulum has a string of length $1.5\,\mathrm{m}$ making $30^\circ$ with the vertical. What is the period of its horizontal circular motion?
items.explain:
Vertical: $T\cos\theta=mg$. Horizontal: $T\sin\theta=m\omega^2r$ with $r=L\sin\theta$. Dividing, $\omega^2=\dfrac{g}{L\cos\theta}$.
$T=2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{L\cos\theta}{g}}=2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{1.5(0.866)}{9.8}}=2.29\,\mathrm{s}$. Check: $v=\sqrt{gr\tan\theta}=2.06\,\mathrm{m/s}$ and $T=2\pi r/v=2.29\,\mathrm{s}$.
items.src: Generated, same style as: Lecture 5 (dynamics of circular motion)

items.q: In a rotor ride a person is pressed against the vertical wall of a cylinder of radius $3.0\,\mathrm{m}$ (coefficient of static friction $0.40$). What is the minimum angular speed that stops the person from sliding down?
items.explain:
Vertical: friction holds the weight, $\mu N\ge mg$. Horizontal: the wall's normal force supplies the centripetal force, $N=m\omega^2R$.
$\mu\omega^2R\ge g\Rightarrow\omega\ge\sqrt{\dfrac{g}{\mu R}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{9.8}{0.40(3.0)}}=2.86\,\mathrm{rad/s}$ (about $27\,\mathrm{rpm}$).
items.src: Generated, same style as: Lecture 5 (dynamics of circular motion)

items.q: A car crosses the top of a circular hill of radius $40\,\mathrm{m}$. What is the greatest speed at which the tyres stay in contact with the road?
items.explain: The road's push vanishes when the whole weight is needed for the centripetal force: $mg=\dfrac{mv^2}{R}\Rightarrow v=\sqrt{gR}=\sqrt{9.8(40)}=19.8\,\mathrm{m/s}$.
items.src: Generated, same style as: Mechanics tutorial Part 5, Q11

items.q: A $0.50\,\mathrm{kg}$ ball on a $1.0\,\mathrm{m}$ string is whirled in a vertical circle and has speed $6.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$ at the top. What is the tension at the top?
items.explain: Both tension and weight point towards the centre at the top: $T+mg=\dfrac{mv^2}{R}\Rightarrow T=0.50\left(\dfrac{36}{1.0}-9.8\right)=13.1\,\mathrm{N}$.
items.src: Generated, same style as: Mechanics tutorial Part 5, Q10

items.q: A grinding wheel spinning at $40\,\mathrm{rad/s}$ is slowed by friction with a constant angular acceleration of $-5.0\,\mathrm{rad/s^2}$. How many revolutions does it make before it stops?
items.explain:
$\omega^2=\omega_0^2+2\alpha\theta\Rightarrow\theta=\dfrac{40^2}{2(5.0)}=160\,\mathrm{rad}$.
Revolutions $=\dfrac{160}{2\pi}=25.5$. Time to stop $=8.0\,\mathrm{s}$; check $\theta=\tfrac12\omega_0t=160\,\mathrm{rad}$.

items.q: A disk speeds up uniformly from $300$ rpm to $900$ rpm in $6.0\,\mathrm{s}$. What is its angular acceleration?
items.explain:
Convert first: $300\,\mathrm{rpm}=31.4\,\mathrm{rad/s}$, $900\,\mathrm{rpm}=94.2\,\mathrm{rad/s}$.
$\alpha=\dfrac{94.2-31.4}{6.0}=10.5\,\mathrm{rad/s^2}$.

items.q: A point on the Earth's equator (radius $6.37\times10^{6}\,\mathrm{m}$) moves in a circle once every $24\,\mathrm{h}$. What is its speed due to the Earth's rotation?
items.explain: $v=\omega R=\dfrac{2\pi}{86400}(6.37\times10^{6})=463\,\mathrm{m/s}$ (about $1670\,\mathrm{km/h}$).

items.q: A bicycle wheel of radius $0.35\,\mathrm{m}$ turns through $3.2\,\mathrm{rad}$. How far does a point on the rim travel along its circular path?
items.explain: $s=r\theta=0.35\times3.2=1.12\,\mathrm{m}$ (the angle must be in radians).

items.q: A car goes round a level curve at constant speed. If the speed is doubled, the friction force needed to keep it on the same curve is multiplied by
items.explain: $f=\dfrac{mv^2}{R}$: it grows with the square of the speed, so doubling $v$ needs four times the friction (which is why the maximum safe speed $\sqrt{\mu gR}$ matters).

items.q: If the radius of a circular path is doubled while the speed stays the same, the centripetal acceleration
items.explain: $a_c=\dfrac{v^2}{r}$: with $v$ fixed it is inversely proportional to $r$.

items.q: A particle moves in a circle with constant speed. The angle between its velocity and its acceleration is
items.explain: Constant speed means no tangential acceleration; the only acceleration is centripetal, perpendicular ($90^\circ$) to the velocity.

items.q: At $20^\circ\mathrm{C}$ a rod is exactly $20.05\,\mathrm{cm}$ long on a steel ruler. Both are placed in an oven at $270^\circ\mathrm{C}$, where the rod measures $20.11\,\mathrm{cm}$ on the same ruler. The coefficient of linear expansion of steel is $11\times10^{-6}\,/^\circ\mathrm{C}$. What is the coefficient of linear expansion of the rod?
items.explain:
The ruler has expanded too, so $20.11$ 'cm' on the hot ruler is longer than $20.11$ true cm: the true length is $20.11(1+11\times10^{-6}\times250)=20.165\,\mathrm{cm}$.
$\alpha=\dfrac{\Delta L}{L_0\Delta T}=\dfrac{20.165-20.05}{20.05\times250}=2.3\times10^{-5}\,/^\circ\mathrm{C}$.
Shortcut: $\alpha_{\text{rod}}\approx\alpha_{\text{apparent}}+\alpha_{\text{steel}}=1.2\times10^{-5}+1.1\times10^{-5}$.

items.q: A steel rail is 30 m long at 10°C. By how much (in millimetres) does it lengthen when heated by 40 °C? (α = 1.2\times10^{-5} per °C)
items.explain: $\Delta L=\alpha L_0\Delta T=1.2\times10^{-5}\times30\times40=0.0144\,\mathrm{m}=14.4\,\mathrm{mm}$.
items.src: Generated, same style as: Thermodynamics tutorial Part I, Q1

items.q: A steel rail is 1000 m long at 10°C. By how much (in millimetres) does it lengthen when heated by 35 °C? (α = 1.1\times10^{-5} per °C)
items.explain: $\Delta L=\alpha L_0\Delta T=1.1\times10^{-5}\times1000\times35=0.385\,\mathrm{m}=385\,\mathrm{mm}$.

items.q: The coefficient of linear expansion of a metal is $24\times10^{-6}\,/^\circ\mathrm{C}$. What is its coefficient of volume expansion?
items.explain: For an isotropic solid $\beta\approx3\alpha=72\times10^{-6}\,/^\circ\mathrm{C}$ (volume = length $\times$ width $\times$ height, each expanding by $\alpha\Delta T$).

items.q: A temperature of $68^\circ\mathrm{F}$ is the same as what temperature on the Kelvin scale?
items.explain: $T_C=\tfrac59(68-32)=20^\circ\mathrm{C}$, then $T=20+273.15=293\,\mathrm{K}$.

items.q: Which pair of temperature changes is equal?
opts: a change of $1\,\mathrm{K}$ and a change of $1^\circ\mathrm{C}$
a change of $1\,\mathrm{K}$ and a change of $1^\circ\mathrm{F}$
a change of $1^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and a change of $1^\circ\mathrm{F}$
items.explain: The Kelvin and Celsius degrees have the same size (only the zero differs by $273.15$), while one Fahrenheit degree is $5/9$ of that.

items.q: If body A is in thermal equilibrium with body C, and body B is in thermal equilibrium with C, then A and B are in thermal equilibrium with each other. This is
items.explain: This transitivity is the zeroth law; it is what makes temperature (and thermometers) meaningful.

items.q: A substance has molar mass $50.0\,\mathrm{g/mol}$. When $314\,\mathrm{J}$ of heat is added to a $30.0\,\mathrm{g}$ sample, its temperature rises from $25.0^\circ\mathrm{C}$ to $45.0^\circ\mathrm{C}$. What is the specific heat of the substance?
For the same substance (specific heat $523\,\mathrm{J/(kg\,K)}$, molar mass $50.0\,\mathrm{g/mol}$), what is the MOLAR specific heat?
items.explain: $C=c\,M=523\times0.0500\,\mathrm{kg/mol}=26.2\,\mathrm{J/(mol\,K)}$ (convert $50.0\,\mathrm{g}$ to $0.0500\,\mathrm{kg}$).

items.q: How many moles are in the $30.0\,\mathrm{g}$ sample of the substance with molar mass $50.0\,\mathrm{g/mol}$?

What mass of steam at $100^\circ\mathrm{C}$ must be mixed with $150\,\mathrm{g}$ of ice at its melting point, in a thermally insulated container, to produce liquid water at $50^\circ\mathrm{C}$? ($L_f=333\,\mathrm{kJ/kg}$, $L_v=2256\,\mathrm{kJ/kg}$, $c_w=4186\,\mathrm{J/(kg\,K)}$)
items.explain:
Heat the ice needs: melt $0.150(333\,\mathrm{kJ})=49.95\,\mathrm{kJ}$ and warm the meltwater $0.150(4186)(50)=31.4\,\mathrm{kJ}$; total $81.3\,\mathrm{kJ}$.
Heat each kg of steam gives: condense $2256\,\mathrm{kJ}$ and cool $4186(50)=209\,\mathrm{kJ}$: $2465\,\mathrm{kJ/kg}$.
$m=\dfrac{81.3}{2465}=0.0330\,\mathrm{kg}=33.0\,\mathrm{g}$.

items.q: 0.25 kg of water at 80 °C is mixed with 0.4 kg of water at 20 °C in an insulated container. What is the final temperature (°C)?
items.explain:
Heat lost by the hot water = heat gained by the cold: $m_wc(T_w-T_f)=m_cc(T_f-T_c)$.
$T_f=\dfrac{m_wT_w+m_cT_c}{m_w+m_c}=\dfrac{0.25(80)+0.4(20)}{0.65}=43.1^\circ\mathrm{C}$.
items.src: Generated, same style as: Thermodynamics tutorial Part I, Q3

items.q: 0.1 kg of water at 90 °C is mixed with 0.3 kg of water at 10 °C in an insulated container. What is the final temperature (°C)?
items.explain:
Heat lost by the hot water = heat gained by the cold: $m_wc(T_w-T_f)=m_cc(T_f-T_c)$.
$T_f=\dfrac{m_wT_w+m_cT_c}{m_w+m_c}=\dfrac{0.1(90)+0.3(10)}{0.4}=30^\circ\mathrm{C}$.
items.src: Generated, same style as: Thermodynamics tutorial Part I, Q3

items.q: How much heat is needed to raise the temperature of a 0.5 kg metal block (c = 900 J/(kg·K)) from 20 °C to 120 °C?
items.explain: $Q=mc\Delta T=0.5\times900\times100=4.5\times10^{4}\,\mathrm{J}$.
items.src: Generated, same style as: Thermodynamics tutorial Part I, Q2

items.q: How much heat is needed to raise the temperature of a 2 kg metal block (c = 385 J/(kg·K)) from 25 °C to 100 °C?
items.explain: $Q=mc\Delta T=2\times385\times75=5.78\times10^{4}\,\mathrm{J}$.
items.src: Generated, same style as: Thermodynamics tutorial Part I, Q2

items.q: How much heat turns $200\,\mathrm{g}$ of ice at $-10^\circ\mathrm{C}$ into steam at $100^\circ\mathrm{C}$? ($c_{\text{ice}}=2090$, $c_w=4186\,\mathrm{J/(kg\,K)}$, $L_f=333\,\mathrm{kJ/kg}$, $L_v=2256\,\mathrm{kJ/kg}$)
items.explain:
Four stages: warm the ice $0.2(2090)(10)=4.2\,\mathrm{kJ}$; melt it $0.2(333)=66.6\,\mathrm{kJ}$; warm the water $0.2(4186)(100)=83.7\,\mathrm{kJ}$; boil it $0.2(2256)=451.2\,\mathrm{kJ}$.
Total $=605.7\,\mathrm{kJ}$. During melting and boiling the temperature stays constant, so $mc\Delta T$ must not be used for those stages.

items.q: Which of the following is the unit of specific heat?
items.explain: $c=\dfrac{Q}{m\Delta T}$ has units $\dfrac{\mathrm{J}}{\mathrm{kg}\,{}^\circ\mathrm{C}}$.

items.q: Identify the intensive (intrinsic) properties.
items.explain: Intensive properties do not depend on the amount of matter; volume, mass, size and length do (extensive).

items.q: A gas expands from $V_0=1.0\,\mathrm{m^3}$ to $4.0V_0$ while its pressure falls from $p_0=40\,\mathrm{Pa}$ to $p_0/4$. Path A: expansion at constant pressure $p_0$, then pressure drop at constant volume. How much work does the gas do along path A?
items.explain:
Work by the gas = area under the path in the $p$-$V$ diagram.
Path A (expansion at $40\,\mathrm{Pa}$, then an isochoric pressure drop): $W=40\times3.0=120\,\mathrm{J}$.
Path B (straight line): $W=\tfrac12(40+10)\times3.0=75\,\mathrm{J}$.
Path C (pressure drop at $1.0\,\mathrm{m^3}$ first, then expansion at $10\,\mathrm{Pa}$): $W=10\times3.0=30\,\mathrm{J}$.

items.q: Suppose $200\,\mathrm{J}$ of work is done ON a system and $70.0\,\mathrm{cal}$ is extracted from it as heat. With $W$ the work done BY the system, what is $\Delta E_{\text{int}}$ (in joules)?
items.explain:
$W=-200\,\mathrm{J}$ (work done on the system is negative work by it); $Q=-70.0\,\mathrm{cal}=-293\,\mathrm{J}$ (heat leaving).
$\Delta E_{\text{int}}=Q-W=-293-(-200)=-93\,\mathrm{J}$.

items.q: A closed gas cycle consists of constant-volume heating AB (heat added $20.0\,\mathrm{J}$), an adiabatic process BC and a constant-pressure compression CA. The net work done during the whole cycle is $15.0\,\mathrm{J}$. How much heat is transferred during CA?
items.explain:
Cycle: $\Delta E_{\text{int}}=0\Rightarrow Q_{\text{net}}=W_{\text{net}}=15.0\,\mathrm{J}$.
$Q_{AB}+Q_{BC}+Q_{CA}=20.0+0+Q_{CA}=15.0\Rightarrow Q_{CA}=-5.0\,\mathrm{J}$ (heat leaves the gas).

items.q: A system absorbs $50\,\mathrm{J}$ of heat and does $11\,\mathrm{J}$ of work. It then follows a different path between the same two states and does $15\,\mathrm{J}$ of work. How much heat is transferred on the second path?
items.explain:
$\Delta E_{\text{int}}=50-11=39\,\mathrm{J}$ is fixed by the end states.
Second path: $Q=\Delta E_{\text{int}}+W=39+15=54\,\mathrm{J}$.

items.q: A system receives $315\,\mathrm{cal}$ of heat and does $20\,\mathrm{cal}$ of work. What is the change in its internal energy (in cal)?
items.explain: $\Delta E_{\text{int}}=Q-W=315-20=295\,\mathrm{cal}$.

items.q: The latent heat of vaporisation of water is $2240\,\mathrm{J}$ per gram. If the work done in vaporising $1\,\mathrm{g}$ is $168\,\mathrm{J}$, what is the increase in internal energy?
items.explain: $\Delta E_{\text{int}}=Q-W=2240-168=2072\,\mathrm{J}$: most of the heat raises the internal energy (breaks molecular bonds); a little pushes back the atmosphere.

items.q: Two cylinders A and B of equal capacity are connected through a stopcock. A holds gas, B is evacuated and the whole system is thermally insulated. The stopcock is suddenly opened. The change in the internal energy of the gas is
items.explain: Free expansion into vacuum: $Q=0$ (insulated) and $W=0$ (no opposing force), so $\Delta E_{\text{int}}=0$ (an ideal gas also keeps its temperature).

items.q: In the sense of the first law, work done ON a system and heat flowing INTO it are respectively
items.explain: With $W$ defined as work done BY the system, work done on it is negative. Heat added is positive: $\Delta E_{\text{int}}=Q-W$.

items.q: The change of internal energy in a cyclic process is
items.explain: The system returns to its initial state, and $E_{\text{int}}$ is a state function, so $\Delta E_{\text{int}}=0$ and $Q=W$ over the cycle.

items.q: The first law of thermodynamics expresses the conservation of
items.explain: $\Delta E_{\text{int}}=Q-W$: energy is neither created nor destroyed.

items.q: In a cyclic process the change of internal energy along path abc is $-200\,\mathrm{J}$. Along c to d $180\,\mathrm{J}$ of heat is added and along d to a a further $80\,\mathrm{J}$. If the work done by the gas along cd and da together is $W_{cda}$, find $W_{cda}$.
items.explain:
Around the full cycle $\Delta E_{\text{int}}=0$, so $\Delta E_{ca}=+200\,\mathrm{J}$ (path cda goes from c back to a).
$W_{cda}=Q_{cda}-\Delta E_{cda}=(180+80)-200=60\,\mathrm{J}$.

items.explain:
The enclosed area is a triangle with base $\Delta V=2.0\,\mathrm{m^3}$ and height $\Delta p=40\,\mathrm{Pa}$: area $=\tfrac12(2.0)(40)=40\,\mathrm{J}$.
The loop a-b-c-a runs ANTICLOCKWISE here (right along the bottom, up on the right, back along the diagonal), so the net work done by the gas is negative: $-40\,\mathrm{J}$ (net work is done ON the gas). Clockwise loops give positive work.
