items.q: Going round a closed loop in a $p$-$V$ diagram CLOCKWISE, the net work done by the gas is
opts: positive and equal to the enclosed area
negative and equal to the enclosed area
positive but larger than the enclosed area
items.explain: On the upper (expansion) branch the gas does more work than is done on it on the lower (compression) branch, so $W_{\text{net}}=+$ area. Anticlockwise loops give $-$ area.
items.src: Final tutorial: work in cyclic processes

items.q: Normal human body temperature is $98.6^\circ\mathrm{F}$. What is it on the Celsius scale?
items.explain: $T_C=\tfrac59(T_F-32)=\tfrac59(66.6)=37.0^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

items.q: Absolute zero, the temperature at which an ideal gas would exert zero pressure, is
items.explain: $0\,\mathrm{K}=-273.15^\circ\mathrm{C}$ ($=-459.67^\circ\mathrm{F}$).

items.q: A $100\,\mathrm{m}$ steel bridge ($\alpha=12\times10^{-6}\,/^\circ\mathrm{C}$) goes from $-10^\circ\mathrm{C}$ in winter to $40^\circ\mathrm{C}$ in summer. By how many centimetres does it lengthen?
items.explain:
$\Delta T=40-(-10)=50^\circ\mathrm{C}$ (subtract carefully!).
$\Delta L=\alpha L_0\Delta T=12\times10^{-6}(100)(50)=0.060\,\mathrm{m}=6.0\,\mathrm{cm}$ - hence expansion joints.

items.q: A circular hole in an aluminium plate ($\alpha=23\times10^{-6}\,/^\circ\mathrm{C}$) has diameter $2.725\,\mathrm{cm}$ at $0^\circ\mathrm{C}$. By how much does the diameter of the hole change when the plate is heated to $100^\circ\mathrm{C}$ (in micrometres)?
items.explain:
A hole expands exactly as a disc of the same material would: $\Delta d=\alpha d_0\Delta T=(23\times10^{-6})(2.725\,\mathrm{cm})(100)=6.3\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{cm}=63\,\mu\mathrm{m}$.
The hole gets LARGER (not smaller) - the metal around it expands outwards; $2\alpha\Delta T$ would be the change in area fraction, not diameter.

items.q: A $0.150\,\mathrm{kg}$ piece of metal at $100^\circ\mathrm{C}$ is dropped into $0.200\,\mathrm{kg}$ of water at $20.0^\circ\mathrm{C}$ in an insulated container (ignore the container). The final temperature is $25.0^\circ\mathrm{C}$. What is the specific heat of the metal?
items.explain:
Heat lost by the metal = heat gained by the water: $m_mc_m(100-25.0)=m_wc_w(25.0-20.0)$.
$c_m=\dfrac{0.200(4186)(5.0)}{0.150(75.0)}=372\,\mathrm{J/(kg\,K)}$ (close to copper, $385$).

items.q: A $500\,\mathrm{W}$ heater delivers all its energy to ice at $0^\circ\mathrm{C}$ for $10$ minutes ($L_f=333\,\mathrm{kJ/kg}$). What mass of ice melts?
items.explain:
Energy supplied $=Pt=500\times600=3.0\times10^5\,\mathrm{J}$ (convert minutes to seconds!).
$m=\dfrac{Pt}{L_f}=\dfrac{3.0\times10^5}{3.33\times10^5}=0.90\,\mathrm{kg}$; the temperature stays at $0^\circ\mathrm{C}$ while it melts.

items.q: Two ice cubes (total $20.0\,\mathrm{g}$, at $0^\circ\mathrm{C}$) are dropped into $250\,\mathrm{g}$ of water at $25.0^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Ignoring the glass, what is the final temperature (in $^\circ$C)?
items.explain:
The ice first melts (absorbing $0.020(333\,\mathrm{kJ})=6.66\,\mathrm{kJ}$), then the meltwater warms from $0$ to $T_f$.
$m_wc(25-T_f)=m_iL_f+m_ic\,T_f\Rightarrow T_f=\dfrac{m_wc(25)-m_iL_f}{(m_w+m_i)c}=\dfrac{26.2-6.66}{1.13}=17.3^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

items.q: Which of these quantities is a STATE function of a thermodynamic system?
items.explain: A state function depends only on the present state (p, V, T), not on how it was reached. Heat and work depend on the path; only their difference $Q-W=\Delta E_{\text{int}}$ does not.

items.q: A closed system is one that exchanges
opts: matter with its surroundings but not energy
energy with its surroundings but not matter
items.explain: Open: matter and energy cross the boundary. Closed: energy only. Isolated: neither.

items.q: Which process is closest to being reversible?
opts: an egg breaking on the floor
very slow compression of a gas in a cylinder with a frictionless piston, always in near equilibrium
a gas rushing into a vacuum
items.explain: A reversible process is a sequence of near-equilibrium states that can be undone by an infinitesimal change in conditions. Free expansion, stirring (friction) and breaking are irreversible.
items.src: Final tutorial: reversible and irreversible processes

items.q: A gas is compressed adiabatically. Its internal energy
items.explain: $Q=0$ and work is done ON the gas ($W<0$), so $\Delta E_{\text{int}}=Q-W=-W>0$: the gas heats up (a bicycle pump becomes warm).

items.q: One mole of an ideal gas expands isothermally. Which statement about the first law is correct?
opts: $\Delta E_{\text{int}}=0$, so all the heat absorbed becomes work done by the gas
$W=0$ so all the heat goes into the internal energy
items.explain: For an ideal gas $E_{\text{int}}$ depends on $T$ only; constant $T$ gives $\Delta E_{\text{int}}=0$ and so $Q=W$.
items.src: Final tutorial: work in special cases

items.q: A gas at $2.0\times10^5\,\mathrm{Pa}$ is heated at constant volume $0.050\,\mathrm{m^3}$ until its pressure doubles. How much work does the gas do?
items.explain: Constant volume: $\Delta V=0$, so $W=p\Delta V=0$; all the heat added increases the internal energy.
items.src: Final tutorial: work done - special cases

items.q: Oxygen of volume $1000\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ at $40.0^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and $1.01\times10^{5}\,\mathrm{Pa}$ expands until its volume is $1500\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ and its pressure is $1.06\times10^{5}\,\mathrm{Pa}$. How many moles of oxygen are present?
items.explain:
$n=\dfrac{pV}{RT}=\dfrac{(1.01\times10^5)(1.000\times10^{-3})}{(8.314)(313.15)}=3.88\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm{mol}$.
Use SI units: $1000\,\mathrm{cm^3}=1.000\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m^3}$ and kelvins.

items.q: For the same oxygen sample (from $1.01\times10^5\,\mathrm{Pa}$, $1000\,\mathrm{cm^3}$, $40.0^\circ\mathrm{C}$ to $1.06\times10^5\,\mathrm{Pa}$, $1500\,\mathrm{cm^3}$), what is the final temperature?
items.explain:
The amount of gas is fixed: $\dfrac{p_1V_1}{T_1}=\dfrac{p_2V_2}{T_2}$.
$T_2=313.15\times\dfrac{1.06\times1500}{1.01\times1000}=493\,\mathrm{K}$ ($220^\circ\mathrm{C}$).

items.q: A quantity of ideal gas at $10.0^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and $100\,\mathrm{kPa}$ occupies $2.50\,\mathrm{m^3}$. How many moles are present?

That gas (initially $2.50\,\mathrm{m^3}$ at $100\,\mathrm{kPa}$, $10.0^\circ\mathrm{C}$) is compressed to $300\,\mathrm{kPa}$ and heated to $30.0^\circ\mathrm{C}$ with no leaks. What volume does it occupy?
items.explain: $V_2=V_1\dfrac{p_1}{p_2}\dfrac{T_2}{T_1}=2.50\times\dfrac13\times\dfrac{303.15}{283.15}=0.892\,\mathrm{m^3}$. Temperatures must be in kelvin.

items.q: The best laboratory vacuum has a pressure of about $1.01\times10^{-13}\,\mathrm{Pa}$. How many gas molecules per cubic centimetre are there at $293\,\mathrm{K}$?
Suppose $1.80\,\mathrm{mol}$ of an ideal gas is compressed isothermally at $30^\circ\mathrm{C}$ from $3.00\,\mathrm{m^3}$ to $1.50\,\mathrm{m^3}$. How much energy is transferred as heat?
items.explain:
Isothermal ideal gas: $\Delta E_{\text{int}}=0$, so $Q=W=nRT\ln\dfrac{V_f}{V_i}=1.80(8.314)(303.15)\ln(0.5)=-3.14\times10^3\,\mathrm{J}$.
Negative: $3140\,\mathrm{J}$ of heat leaves the gas (transfer FROM the gas to the surroundings).

items.q: In an isothermal compression of an ideal gas, the heat transfer is
opts: equal to the increase in internal energy
from the gas to the surroundings
from the surroundings to the gas
items.explain: $\Delta E_{\text{int}}=0$ and $W<0$ (work done on the gas) give $Q=W<0$: heat flows out of the gas.

items.q: An air bubble of volume $20\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ is at the bottom of a lake $40\,\mathrm{m}$ deep, where the temperature is $4.0^\circ\mathrm{C}$. It rises to the surface, at $20^\circ\mathrm{C}$, with the same temperature as the water. What is its volume at the surface?
items.explain:
Pressure at depth: $p_1=p_0+\rho gh=1.013\times10^5+(1000)(9.8)(40)=4.93\times10^5\,\mathrm{Pa}$.
$V_2=V_1\dfrac{p_1}{p_2}\dfrac{T_2}{T_1}=20\times\dfrac{4.93}{1.013}\times\dfrac{293.15}{277.15}=1.0\times10^2\,\mathrm{cm^3}$.

items.q: Container A holds an ideal gas at $5.0\times10^5\,\mathrm{Pa}$ and $300\,\mathrm{K}$; container B, with four times the volume, holds the same gas at $1.0\times10^5\,\mathrm{Pa}$ and $400\,\mathrm{K}$. A valve between them is opened; the temperature of each container is maintained. What is the final pressure?
items.explain:
Moles add: $\dfrac{p_AV}{RT_A}+\dfrac{p_B(4V)}{RT_B}=\dfrac{p\,V}{RT_A}+\dfrac{p\,(4V)}{RT_B}$.
$p=\dfrac{p_A/T_A+4p_B/T_B}{1/T_A+4/T_B}=\dfrac{1667+1000}{0.003333+0.01}=2.0\times10^5\,\mathrm{Pa}$.

items.q: What is the rms speed of a nitrogen molecule ($M=28\,\mathrm{g/mol}$) at $20.0^\circ\mathrm{C}$?
items.explain:
$v_{\text{rms}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{3RT}{M}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{3(8.314)(293.15)}{0.028}}=511\,\mathrm{m/s}$. Use kelvins and kg/mol.
Cross-check with $m=M/N_A$ and $k_B$: $\sqrt{3k_BT/m}$ gives the same value.

items.q: At what temperature is the rms speed of nitrogen molecules half its value at $20.0^\circ\mathrm{C}$?
items.explain: $v_{\text{rms}}\propto\sqrt T$, so half the speed needs a quarter of the temperature: $T=293.15/4=73.3\,\mathrm{K}$ ($-200^\circ\mathrm{C}$).

items.q: At what temperature is the rms speed of nitrogen molecules twice its value at $20.0^\circ\mathrm{C}$?
items.explain: Double the speed needs four times the (absolute) temperature: $T=4(293.15)=1173\,\mathrm{K}$ ($899^\circ\mathrm{C}$).

items.q: At $273\,\mathrm{K}$ and $1.00\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm{atm}$ the density of a gas is $1.24\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$. What is the rms speed of its molecules?
items.explain:
$p=\tfrac13\rho v_{\text{rms}}^2\Rightarrow v_{\text{rms}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{3p}{\rho}}$ with $p=1.013\times10^3\,\mathrm{Pa}$ and $\rho=1.24\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}$.
$v_{\text{rms}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{3(1013)}{0.0124}}=495\,\mathrm{m/s}$.

items.q: For that gas (density $1.24\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$ at $273\,\mathrm{K}$ and $1.00\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm{atm}$), what is the molar mass in g/mol?
items.explain:
$M=\dfrac{\rho RT}{p}=\dfrac{(0.0124)(8.314)(273)}{1013}=0.0278\,\mathrm{kg/mol}=27.8\,\mathrm{g/mol}$.
That matches nitrogen $\mathrm{N_2}$ ($28.0\,\mathrm{g/mol}$; CO is also close).
items.src: Thermodynamics tutorial Part II (1), Q10(b, c)

items.q: What is the average translational kinetic energy of an ideal-gas molecule at 0.00 °C?
items.explain: $\bar K=\tfrac32k_BT=\tfrac32(1.38\times10^{-23})(273.15)=5.65\times10^{-21}\,\mathrm{J}$ ($=0.0353\,\mathrm{eV}$). It depends on temperature only, not on the gas.
items.src: Thermodynamics tutorial Part II (1), Q11(a, b)

items.q: What is the average translational kinetic energy of an ideal-gas molecule at 100 °C?
items.explain: $\bar K=\tfrac32k_BT=\tfrac32(1.38\times10^{-23})(373.15)=7.72\times10^{-21}\,\mathrm{J}$ ($=0.0482\,\mathrm{eV}$). It depends on temperature only, not on the gas.
items.src: Thermodynamics tutorial Part II (1), Q11(a, b)

items.q: What is the translational kinetic energy per MOLE of an ideal gas at 0 °C?
items.explain: $K_{\text{mol}}=\tfrac32RT=\tfrac32(8.314)(273.15)=3410\,\mathrm{J/mol}$.
items.src: Thermodynamics tutorial Part II (1), Q11(c, d)

items.q: What is the translational kinetic energy per MOLE of an ideal gas at 100 °C?
items.explain: $K_{\text{mol}}=\tfrac32RT=\tfrac32(8.314)(373.15)=4650\,\mathrm{J/mol}$.
items.src: Thermodynamics tutorial Part II (1), Q11(c, d)

items.q: The heat of vaporisation of water ($539\,\mathrm{cal/g}$) is approximately $\varepsilon n$, where $\varepsilon$ is the average energy of an escaping molecule and $n$ the number of molecules per gram. Find $\varepsilon$ (molar mass of $\mathrm{H_2O}$: $18.0\,\mathrm{g/mol}$).
items.explain:
Molecules per gram $n=\dfrac{N_A}{18.0}=3.35\times10^{22}$; $L=539(4.186)=2256\,\mathrm{J/g}$.
$\varepsilon=\dfrac{L}{n}=\dfrac{2256}{3.35\times10^{22}}=6.7\times10^{-20}\,\mathrm{J}$ ($0.42\,\mathrm{eV}$).

items.q: The escaping water molecules have average energy $\varepsilon=6.7\times10^{-20}\,\mathrm{J}$. What is the ratio of $\varepsilon$ to the average kinetic energy $\tfrac32kT$ of water molecules at $32.0^\circ\mathrm{C}$?
items.explain:
$\tfrac32kT=\tfrac32(1.38\times10^{-23})(305.15)=6.3\times10^{-21}\,\mathrm{J}$.
$\dfrac{\varepsilon}{\bar K}=\dfrac{6.7\times10^{-20}}{6.3\times10^{-21}}\approx11$: only the unusually energetic molecules escape.

items.q: What is the mean free path of oxygen molecules (diameter $3.0\times10^{-8}\,\mathrm{cm}$) at $1.0\,\mathrm{atm}$ and $0^\circ\mathrm{C}$?
items.explain:
$\dfrac NV=\dfrac{p}{kT}=2.69\times10^{25}\,\mathrm{m^{-3}}$.
$\lambda=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2\,\pi d^2(N/V)}=\dfrac{1}{1.414\pi(3.0\times10^{-10})^2(2.69\times10^{25})}=9.3\times10^{-8}\,\mathrm{m}$.

items.q: At what frequency would the wavelength of sound in air (speed $331\,\mathrm{m/s}$ at $0^\circ\mathrm{C}$) equal the mean free path of oxygen molecules, $9.3\times10^{-8}\,\mathrm{m}$?
items.explain: $f=\dfrac{v}{\lambda}=\dfrac{331}{9.3\times10^{-8}}=3.6\times10^{9}\,\mathrm{Hz}$ (far into the ultrasonic range: sound cannot propagate when its wavelength is below the mean free path).

items.q: In a particle accelerator the residual gas is at $295\,\mathrm{K}$ and $1.00\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{torr}$ ($1\,\mathrm{torr}=133.3\,\mathrm{Pa}$). How many gas molecules are there per cubic centimetre?
For molecules of diameter $2.0\times10^{-8}\,\mathrm{cm}$ at $3.3\times10^{16}\,\mathrm{molecules/m^3}$, what is the mean free path?
items.explain: $\lambda=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2\pi d^2(N/V)}=\dfrac{1}{1.414\pi(2.0\times10^{-10})^2(3.27\times10^{16})}=1.7\times10^{2}\,\mathrm{m}$ - much longer than the $23.0\,\mathrm{m}$ diameter of the ring, so protons rarely hit residual gas.

items.q: At $20^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and $750\,\mathrm{torr}$ the mean free paths of argon and nitrogen are $9.9\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{cm}$ and $27.5\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{cm}$. What is the ratio of the diameter of an argon atom to that of an $\mathrm{N_2}$ molecule?
items.explain: $\lambda=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2\pi d^2(N/V)}\propto\dfrac1{d^2}$ at equal $p$ and $T$, so $\dfrac{d_{Ar}}{d_{N_2}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{\lambda_{N_2}}{\lambda_{Ar}}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{27.5}{9.9}}=1.67$.

items.q: The mean free path of argon is $9.9\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{cm}$ at $20^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and $750\,\mathrm{torr}$. What is it at $20^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and $150\,\mathrm{torr}$ (in cm)?
items.explain: At fixed $T$, $\lambda\propto1/p$: the pressure is $5$ times lower, so the mean free path is $5$ times longer: $4.95\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{cm}$.

items.q: The mean free path of argon is $9.9\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{cm}$ at $20^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and $750\,\mathrm{torr}$. What is it at $-40^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and $750\,\mathrm{torr}$ (in cm)?
items.explain: At fixed $p$, $\lambda\propto T$ (the density $N/V=p/kT$ is higher when colder): $\lambda=9.9\times10^{-6}\,\dfrac{233.15}{293.15}=7.9\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{cm}$.

items.q: The mean free path of a gas molecule is $\lambda_1$ at temperature $T$. If the pressure and the absolute temperature are both doubled, the new mean free path is
items.explain: $\lambda\propto\dfrac{T}{p}$: doubling both leaves the ratio, hence $\lambda$, unchanged.

items.q: The speeds of 22 particles are: 2 particles at $1.0\,\mathrm{cm/s}$, 4 at $2.0$, 6 at $3.0$, 8 at $4.0$ and 2 at $5.0\,\mathrm{cm/s}$. What is the average speed?
For the same 22 particles, what is the rms speed?
For the same 22 particles, what is the most probable speed?
items.explain: The most probable speed is the one shared by the most particles: $8$ particles have $4.0\,\mathrm{cm/s}$.

items.q: The most probable speed of the molecules in a gas at temperature $T_2$ equals the rms speed at temperature $T_1$. What is $T_2/T_1$?
items.explain: $v_p=\sqrt{\dfrac{2kT_2}{m}}$ and $v_{\text{rms}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{3kT_1}{m}}$. Equal speeds give $2T_2=3T_1$, so $\dfrac{T_2}{T_1}=\dfrac32=1.5$.

items.q: The quantity $pV/kT$ ($k$ = Boltzmann's constant) represents
opts: the total mass of the gas
the number of moles of the gas
the number of molecules in the gas
items.explain: $pV=NkT\Rightarrow\dfrac{pV}{kT}=N$, the number of molecules (compare $pV/RT=n$, the number of moles).

items.q: For an ideal gas at constant temperature ($pV=\text{constant}$), the graph of pressure $p$ against density $\rho$ is
opts: a straight line through the origin
a straight line parallel to the $p$-axis
a straight line parallel to the $\rho$-axis
items.explain: $p=\dfrac{\rho RT}{M}$: pressure is proportional to density at fixed temperature.

items.q: The rms speed of the molecules of a gas is $300\,\mathrm{m/s}$. If the absolute temperature is halved and the molecular weight doubled, the rms speed becomes
items.explain: $v_{\text{rms}}\propto\sqrt{T/M}$; the factor is $\sqrt{\tfrac12/2}=\tfrac12$, so $v=150\,\mathrm{m/s}$.

items.q: The average translational kinetic energy of the molecules of an ideal gas is
opts: proportional to the square root of the temperature
inversely proportional to the absolute temperature
directly proportional to the absolute temperature
items.explain: $\bar K=\tfrac32k_BT$.

items.q: The specific heat of a gas in an ISOTHERMAL process is
items.explain: $c=\dfrac{Q}{m\Delta T}$ with $\Delta T=0$ but $Q\ne0$: formally infinite.

items.q: The specific heat of a gas in an ADIABATIC process is
items.explain: $Q=0$ with $\Delta T\ne0$, so $c=0$.

items.q: An ideal gas in a sealed container is heated at constant volume from $300\,\mathrm{K}$ to $600\,\mathrm{K}$. The mean kinetic energy of its molecules
items.explain: $\bar K=\tfrac32kT$ is proportional to the absolute temperature, which doubled.

items.q: $70\,\mathrm{cal}$ of heat raises the temperature of $2$ moles of an ideal diatomic gas by $5^\circ\mathrm{C}$ at constant pressure. How much heat would raise the temperature of the same gas through the same range at constant volume?
items.explain:
$\dfrac{Q_V}{Q_p}=\dfrac{C_V}{C_p}=\dfrac{5/2}{7/2}=\dfrac57$ for a diatomic gas (rotation but no vibration).
$Q_V=70\times\dfrac57=50\,\mathrm{cal}$.

items.q: A hydrogen molecule ($\mathrm{H_2}$, $M=2.016\,\mathrm{g/mol}$) escapes from a $4000\,\mathrm{K}$ furnace travelling at the rms speed. What is that speed?

The hydrogen molecule ($\mathrm{d}=1.0\times10^{-8}\,\mathrm{cm}$, speed $7.03\times10^{3}\,\mathrm{m/s}$) moves through cold argon atoms ($d=3.0\times10^{-8}\,\mathrm{cm}$) at $4.0\times10^{19}\,\mathrm{atoms/cm^3}$. How many collisions per second does it initially experience?
items.explain:
A collision happens when the centres come within $r_1+r_2=\tfrac12(d_1+d_2)=2.0\times10^{-10}\,\mathrm{m}$: cross-section $\sigma=\pi(2.0\times10^{-10})^2$.
Rate $=n_{Ar}\sigma v=(4.0\times10^{25})(1.26\times10^{-19})(7.03\times10^3)=3.5\times10^{10}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$.

items.q: What is the internal energy of $1.0\,\mathrm{mol}$ of an ideal MONATOMIC gas at $273\,\mathrm{K}$?

One mole of an ideal DIATOMIC gas (rotation, no vibration) goes from a ($2.0\,\mathrm{m^3}$, $5.0\,\mathrm{kPa}$) to c ($4.0\,\mathrm{m^3}$, $2.0\,\mathrm{kPa}$). What is the change in its internal energy?
items.explain: $\Delta E_{\text{int}}=nC_V\Delta T=\tfrac52\,\Delta(pV)$ (since $pV=nRT$) $=2.5(2000\times4.0-5000\times2.0)=-5.0\times10^3\,\mathrm{J}$.

items.explain:
Work = area under the diagonal $=\tfrac12(5.0+2.0)\,\mathrm{kPa}\times2.0\,\mathrm{m^3}=7.0\,\mathrm{kJ}$.
$Q=\Delta E_{\text{int}}+W=-5.0+7.0=+2.0\,\mathrm{kJ}=2.0\times10^{3}\,\mathrm{J}$.

items.q: A container holds three non-reacting gases: $2.40\,\mathrm{mol}$ with $C_V=12.0$, $1.50\,\mathrm{mol}$ with $C_V=12.8$ and $3.20\,\mathrm{mol}$ with $C_V=20.0\,\mathrm{J/(mol\,K)}$. What is $C_V$ of the mixture?
items.explain: Heat capacities add: $C_V^{\text{mix}}=\dfrac{\sum n_iC_{Vi}}{\sum n_i}=\dfrac{28.8+19.2+64.0}{7.10}=15.8\,\mathrm{J/(mol\,K)}$ (a mole-weighted average, not a plain mean).

items.q: $70\,\mathrm{J}$ is added as heat to a diatomic gas (rotating, not oscillating) which then expands at constant pressure. By how much does its internal energy increase?
items.explain: Constant pressure: $Q=nC_p\Delta T$ and $\Delta E_{\text{int}}=nC_V\Delta T$, so $\Delta E_{\text{int}}=Q\dfrac{C_V}{C_p}=70\times\dfrac{5}{7}=50\,\mathrm{J}$ (the other $20\,\mathrm{J}$ is the work of expansion).

items.q: $12.0\,\mathrm{g}$ of oxygen ($\mathrm{O_2}$, $M=32.0\,\mathrm{g/mol}$) is heated at constant atmospheric pressure from $25.0^\circ\mathrm{C}$ to $125^\circ\mathrm{C}$. How much heat is transferred (rotation, no oscillation)?
items.explain:
$n=\dfrac{12.0}{32.0}=0.375\,\mathrm{mol}$ and $C_p=\tfrac72R=29.1\,\mathrm{J/(mol\,K)}$.
$Q=nC_p\Delta T=0.375(29.1)(100)=1.09\times10^3\,\mathrm{J}$.

items.q: In heating oxygen at constant pressure (rotation, no oscillation), what fraction of the heat goes into raising the internal energy?
items.explain: $\dfrac{\Delta E_{\text{int}}}{Q}=\dfrac{C_V}{C_p}=\dfrac{5/2}{7/2}=\dfrac57=0.714$.

items.q: A gas with $\gamma=1.30$, initially at $273\,\mathrm{K}$ and $1.00\,\mathrm{atm}$ ($V=1.00\,\mathrm{L}$), is suddenly compressed adiabatically to half its volume. What is its final pressure (in atm)?
items.explain: Adiabatic: $pV^\gamma=\text{constant}$, so $p_2=p_1\left(\dfrac{V_1}{V_2}\right)^\gamma=1.00(2)^{1.30}=2.46\,\mathrm{atm}$ (more than the isothermal $2.00\,\mathrm{atm}$).

items.q: The gas ($\gamma=1.30$, $273\,\mathrm{K}$) is compressed adiabatically to half its volume. What is its final temperature?
After the adiabatic compression to $336\,\mathrm{K}$ and $0.500\,\mathrm{L}$, the gas is cooled back to $273\,\mathrm{K}$ at constant pressure. What is its final volume (in L)?
items.explain: Constant pressure: $V\propto T$, so $V_3=0.500\,\mathrm{L}\times\dfrac{273}{336}=0.406\,\mathrm{L}$.

items.q: Opening champagne: the gas pocket (mostly $\mathrm{CO_2}$, $\gamma=4/3$) at $5.00\,\mathrm{atm}$ and $5.00^\circ\mathrm{C}$ expands adiabatically to $1.00\,\mathrm{atm}$. What is its final temperature?
items.explain: Adiabatic: $T\,p^{(1-\gamma)/\gamma}=\text{constant}$, so $T_f=T_i\left(\dfrac{p_f}{p_i}\right)^{(\gamma-1)/\gamma}=278.15(0.200)^{0.25}=186\,\mathrm{K}$ ($-87^\circ\mathrm{C}$): the gas cools so much that fog forms.

items.q: Path 1 from state i to state f consists of an isothermal expansion (work $50\,\mathrm{J}$), an adiabatic expansion ($40\,\mathrm{J}$), an isothermal compression ($30\,\mathrm{J}$) and an adiabatic compression ($25\,\mathrm{J}$). What is $\Delta E_{\text{int}}$ along any other path from i to f?
items.explain:
Isothermal steps: $\Delta E_{\text{int}}=0$. Adiabatic expansion: $\Delta E_{\text{int}}=-W=-40\,\mathrm{J}$; adiabatic compression: $+25\,\mathrm{J}$.
$\Delta E_{\text{int}}=-40+25=-15\,\mathrm{J}$ - the same along every path, since $E_{\text{int}}$ is a state function.

items.q: An ideal diatomic gas (rotation, no oscillation) is compressed adiabatically from $1.20\,\mathrm{atm}$ and $0.200\,\mathrm{m^3}$ to $2.40\,\mathrm{atm}$. How much work does the gas do?
items.explain:
$V_2=V_1(p_1/p_2)^{1/\gamma}=0.200(0.5)^{0.714}=0.122\,\mathrm{m^3}$.
$W=\dfrac{p_2V_2-p_1V_1}{1-\gamma}=\dfrac{2.97\times10^4-2.43\times10^4}{-0.4}=-1.33\times10^4\,\mathrm{J}$ (negative: work is done ON the gas). Numerical integration of $\int p\,dV$ along the adiabat gives the same.

items.q: One mole of an ideal monatomic gas follows the cycle 1-2-3-1 shown: 1 to 2 at constant volume ($T_1=300\,\mathrm{K}\to T_2=600\,\mathrm{K}$), 2 to 3 an adiabatic expansion (to $T_3=455\,\mathrm{K}$) and 3 to 1 at constant pressure. How much heat is added during 1 to 2?
items.explain: Constant volume: $Q=nC_V\Delta T=1(1.5)(8.314)(300)=3.74\times10^3\,\mathrm{J}$ (and $W=0$, $\Delta E_{\text{int}}=Q$).

items.q: For the same cycle, how much work does the gas do in the adiabatic expansion 2 to 3 ($600\,\mathrm{K}\to455\,\mathrm{K}$)?
items.explain: Adiabatic: $Q=0\Rightarrow W=-\Delta E_{\text{int}}=-nC_V(T_3-T_2)=-(1.5)(8.314)(455-600)=+1.81\times10^3\,\mathrm{J}$.

items.q: For the same cycle, how much heat is transferred during the isobaric compression 3 to 1 ($455\,\mathrm{K}\to300\,\mathrm{K}$)?
items.explain: Constant pressure: $Q=nC_p\Delta T=(2.5)(8.314)(300-455)=-3.22\times10^3\,\mathrm{J}$ (heat leaves the gas).

items.q: For the same complete cycle, what is the net work done by the gas?
items.explain: Net work $=0+1808+(-1289)\approx+520\,\mathrm{J}$; by the first law this equals the net heat $3741+0-3222\approx520\,\mathrm{J}$ (a closed cycle has $\Delta E_{\text{int}}=0$).

items.q: For an ideal diatomic gas (rotation, no vibration), the molar heat capacity at constant volume is
items.explain: $C_V=\tfrac52R=2.5(8.314)=20.8\,\mathrm{J/(mol\,K)}$ (molar heat capacities have units J/(mol K)).

items.q: A diatomic gas compressed isobarically has $42\,\mathrm{J}$ of work involved. What is the magnitude of the heat exchanged with the gas?
items.explain: Isobaric: $W=nR\Delta T$ and $Q=nC_p\Delta T=\tfrac72nR\Delta T$, so $|Q|=\tfrac72|W|=3.5\times42=147\,\mathrm{J}$ (heat leaves the gas in a compression).

items.q: The adiabatic relation between volume and temperature of an ideal gas is
items.explain: From $pV^\gamma=\text{const}$ and $p=nRT/V$: $TV^{\gamma-1}=\text{constant}$.

items.q: Which statement about $C_p$ and $C_V$ of an ideal gas is correct?
opts: $C_p$ may be less than $C_V$ for some gases
items.explain: Mayer's relation: $C_p-C_V=R>0$. Heating at constant pressure also does expansion work, so more heat is needed per degree.

items.q: For a diatomic gas $\gamma=C_p/C_V$ equals
items.explain: $C_p=\tfrac72R$, $C_V=\tfrac52R$: $\gamma=\tfrac75=1.4$ (monatomic: $\tfrac53$).

items.q: The work done by an ideal gas in an adiabatic expansion from $(p_1,V_1)$ to $(p_2,V_2)$ is
items.explain: $W=-\Delta E_{\text{int}}=-nC_V\Delta T=\dfrac{p_1V_1-p_2V_2}{\gamma-1}=\dfrac{p_2V_2-p_1V_1}{1-\gamma}$.

items.q: A monatomic ideal gas is suddenly compressed adiabatically to $1/8$ of its initial volume. What is the ratio of its final pressure to its initial pressure?
items.explain: $p_2/p_1=(V_1/V_2)^\gamma=8^{5/3}=32$ (an isothermal compression would give only $8$).

items.q: One mole of a monatomic ideal gas is mixed with one mole of a diatomic ideal gas. What is the molar specific heat of the mixture at constant volume?
items.explain: $C_V^{\text{mix}}=\dfrac{1(\tfrac32R)+1(\tfrac52R)}{2}=2R$.

items.q: How much heat is needed to raise the temperature of $2.0\,\mathrm{mol}$ of an ideal monatomic gas by $50\,\mathrm{K}$ at constant volume?
items.explain: $Q=nC_V\Delta T=2.0(\tfrac32\cdot8.314)(50)=1.25\times10^3\,\mathrm{J}$ (all of it raises the internal energy).

items.q: The same $2.0\,\mathrm{mol}$ of monatomic gas is heated by $50\,\mathrm{K}$ at constant PRESSURE. How much heat is needed?
items.explain: $Q=nC_p\Delta T=2.0(\tfrac52\cdot8.314)(50)=2.08\times10^3\,\mathrm{J}$: $1.25\,\mathrm{kJ}$ for the internal energy plus $0.83\,\mathrm{kJ}$ of expansion work $nR\Delta T$.

items.q: Which of these is the equation of state of an ideal gas?
items.explain: $pV=nRT=Nk_BT$.

items.q: A fixed amount of an ideal gas is taken from state A to state B along an isothermal path and then along an adiabatic path ending at the same volume. Starting from the same state and expanding to the same final volume, which path ends at the LOWER temperature?
opts: they end at the same temperature
it depends on the gas but not on the path
items.explain: In an adiabatic expansion the gas does work at the expense of its internal energy, so it cools; in the isothermal expansion heat flows in to keep $T$ constant.

items.q: Four moles of an ideal gas expand reversibly and isothermally at $400\,\mathrm{K}$ to twice their volume. What is the entropy change of the gas?
items.explain:
$\Delta S=nR\ln\dfrac{V_2}{V_1}=4.00(8.314)\ln2=23.1\,\mathrm{J/K}$.
Check with $\Delta S=\dfrac QT$: $Q=W=nRT\ln2=9.22\times10^3\,\mathrm{J}$ and $\dfrac{9220}{400}=23.1\,\mathrm{J/K}$.

items.q: Four moles of an ideal gas at $400\,\mathrm{K}$ double their volume in a reversible isothermal expansion. How much work does the gas do?
If the same expansion (volume doubled) is carried out reversibly and ADIABATICALLY instead, the entropy change of the gas is
items.explain: Reversible adiabatic: $\mathrm{d}S=\dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q_{\text{rev}}}{T}=0$ (isentropic): the volume increase raises the entropy but the cooling lowers it by exactly the same amount.

items.q: An ideal gas expands reversibly and isothermally at $77.0^\circ\mathrm{C}$ from $1.30\,\mathrm{L}$ to $3.40\,\mathrm{L}$, and its entropy change is $22.0\,\mathrm{J/K}$. How many moles of gas are present?
items.explain: $\Delta S=nR\ln\dfrac{V_2}{V_1}\Rightarrow n=\dfrac{22.0}{8.314\ln(3.40/1.30)}=\dfrac{22.0}{7.99}=2.75\,\mathrm{mol}$. (The temperature does not matter for an isothermal $\Delta S$ of an ideal gas.)

items.q: How much heat must be transferred for a reversible isothermal expansion of an ideal gas at $132^\circ\mathrm{C}$ if the entropy of the gas increases by $46.0\,\mathrm{J/K}$?
A $2.00\,\mathrm{kg}$ block of copper ($c=386\,\mathrm{J/(kg\,K)}$) is heated reversibly from $25.0^\circ\mathrm{C}$ to $100^\circ\mathrm{C}$. What is the energy absorbed as heat?
For that copper block (heated reversibly from $298.15\,\mathrm{K}$ to $373.15\,\mathrm{K}$), what is the entropy change?
items.explain:
$\mathrm{d}S=\dfrac{mc\,\mathrm{d}T}{T}$, so $\Delta S=mc\ln\dfrac{T_2}{T_1}=772\ln\dfrac{373.15}{298.15}=173\,\mathrm{J/K}$.
Not $Q/T_{\text{one}}$: the temperature changes during the heating (the answer lies between $Q/T_2=155$ and $Q/T_1=194\,\mathrm{J/K}$). Numerical integration of $\mathrm{d}Q/T$ agrees.

items.q: A $12.0\,\mathrm{g}$ ice cube melts completely in a bucket of water just above the freezing point ($L_f=333\,\mathrm{kJ/kg}$). What is the entropy change of the ice cube?
items.explain: Melting happens at constant $T=273.15\,\mathrm{K}$: $\Delta S=\dfrac{Q}{T}=\dfrac{mL_f}{T}=\dfrac{0.0120(333\,000)}{273.15}=14.6\,\mathrm{J/K}$.

items.q: A $5.00\,\mathrm{g}$ spoonful of water evaporates completely on a hot plate just above the boiling point ($L_v=2256\,\mathrm{kJ/kg}$). What is the entropy change of the water?
items.explain: $\Delta S=\dfrac{mL_v}{T}=\dfrac{0.00500(2.256\times10^6)}{373.15}=30.2\,\mathrm{J/K}$ (positive: more disorder in the vapour).

items.q: A Carnot engine whose low-temperature reservoir is at $17^\circ\mathrm{C}$ has an efficiency of $40\%$. By how much must the temperature of the high-temperature reservoir be increased to raise the efficiency to $50\%$?
items.explain:
$\varepsilon=1-\dfrac{T_L}{T_H}\Rightarrow T_H=\dfrac{T_L}{1-\varepsilon}$ with $T_L=290.15\,\mathrm{K}$.
$T_H=\dfrac{290.15}{0.60}=483.6\,\mathrm{K}$ at $40\%$ and $\dfrac{290.15}{0.50}=580.3\,\mathrm{K}$ at $50\%$: increase $=96.7\,\mathrm{K}$.

items.q: A Carnot engine absorbs $52\,\mathrm{kJ}$ as heat and exhausts $36\,\mathrm{kJ}$ in each cycle. What is its efficiency (%)?
items.explain: $\varepsilon=\dfrac{W}{Q_H}=1-\dfrac{Q_L}{Q_H}=1-\dfrac{36}{52}=0.308=30.8\%$.

items.q: A Carnot engine absorbs $52\,\mathrm{kJ}$ as heat and exhausts $36\,\mathrm{kJ}$ per cycle. How much work does it do per cycle?
A Carnot engine of efficiency $22.0\%$ operates between constant-temperature reservoirs differing by $75.0^\circ\mathrm{C}$. What is the temperature of the HIGH-temperature reservoir (in kelvins)?
items.explain: $\varepsilon=\dfrac{T_H-T_L}{T_H}=\dfrac{75.0}{T_H}\Rightarrow T_H=\dfrac{75.0}{0.220}=341\,\mathrm{K}$ ($67.7^\circ\mathrm{C}$); then $T_L=341-75=266\,\mathrm{K}$ ($-7.3^\circ\mathrm{C}$).

items.q: A car engine has an efficiency of $25\%$ when it does $8.2\,\mathrm{kJ}$ of work per cycle. How much energy does the engine gain per cycle as heat from the fuel?
items.explain: $\varepsilon=\dfrac{W}{Q_{\text{gain}}}\Rightarrow Q_{\text{gain}}=\dfrac{8.2}{0.25}=32.8\,\mathrm{kJ}$; the engine loses $32.8-8.2=24.6\,\mathrm{kJ}$ per cycle.

items.q: After a tune-up the efficiency of the engine rises to $31\%$ at the same work ($8.2\,\mathrm{kJ}$ per cycle). How much heat does it now lose (exhaust) per cycle?
items.explain: $Q_{\text{gain}}=\dfrac{8.2}{0.31}=26.5\,\mathrm{kJ}$, so $Q_{\text{lost}}=26.5-8.2=18.3\,\mathrm{kJ}$ (down from $24.6\,\mathrm{kJ}$).

items.q: A gasoline engine is modelled by the Otto cycle with compression ratio $4.00$ and $\gamma=1.30$. What is its efficiency (%)?
items.explain:
Otto cycle: $\varepsilon=1-\dfrac{T_1}{T_2}=1-r^{1-\gamma}=1-4^{-0.30}=1-0.660=0.340$, i.e. $34.0\%$.
The temperature ratio across the adiabatic compression is $T_2/T_1=r^{\gamma-1}=4^{0.30}=1.52$; $(1-1/r)=75\%$ would be wrong.
items.src: Generated, same style as: Thermodynamics tutorial Part III, Q16(f)

items.q: In the Otto-cycle model of a gasoline engine (compression ratio $4.00$, $\gamma=1.30$), what is the ratio $T_2/T_1$ of the temperatures at the end and the start of the adiabatic compression?
items.explain: Adiabatic: $TV^{\gamma-1}=\text{const}$, so $\dfrac{T_2}{T_1}=\left(\dfrac{V_1}{V_2}\right)^{\gamma-1}=4.00^{0.30}=1.52$.

items.q: How much work must a Carnot refrigerator do to transfer $1.0\,\mathrm{J}$ of heat from a reservoir at 7 °C to one at 27 °C?
items.explain: $K=\dfrac{Q_L}{W}=\dfrac{T_L}{T_H-T_L}\Rightarrow W=Q_L\,\dfrac{T_H-T_L}{T_L}=\dfrac{300.15-280.15}{280.15}=0.0714\,\mathrm{J}$ (kelvins). The colder the cold reservoir, the more work each joule costs.

items.q: How much work must a Carnot refrigerator do to transfer $1.0\,\mathrm{J}$ of heat from a reservoir at -73 °C to one at 27 °C?
items.explain: $K=\dfrac{Q_L}{W}=\dfrac{T_L}{T_H-T_L}\Rightarrow W=Q_L\,\dfrac{T_H-T_L}{T_L}=\dfrac{300.15-200.15}{200.15}=0.5\,\mathrm{J}$ (kelvins). The colder the cold reservoir, the more work each joule costs.

items.q: How much work must a Carnot refrigerator do to transfer $1.0\,\mathrm{J}$ of heat from a reservoir at -173 °C to one at 27 °C?
items.explain: $K=\dfrac{Q_L}{W}=\dfrac{T_L}{T_H-T_L}\Rightarrow W=Q_L\,\dfrac{T_H-T_L}{T_L}=\dfrac{300.15-100.15}{100.15}=2\,\mathrm{J}$ (kelvins). The colder the cold reservoir, the more work each joule costs.

items.q: How much work must a Carnot refrigerator do to transfer $1.0\,\mathrm{J}$ of heat from a reservoir at -223 °C to one at 27 °C?
items.explain: $K=\dfrac{Q_L}{W}=\dfrac{T_L}{T_H-T_L}\Rightarrow W=Q_L\,\dfrac{T_H-T_L}{T_L}=\dfrac{300.15-50.15}{50.15}=4.99\,\mathrm{J}$ (kelvins). The colder the cold reservoir, the more work each joule costs.

items.q: A heat pump with coefficient of performance $3.8$ delivers $7.54\,\mathrm{MJ}$ as heat to a building each hour. At what rate must work be done to run it?
items.explain:
For a heat pump $K=\dfrac{Q_H}{W}$, so $W=\dfrac{7.54\times10^6}{3.8}=1.98\times10^6\,\mathrm{J}$ per hour.
Rate $=\dfrac{1.98\times10^6}{3600}=5.5\times10^2\,\mathrm{W}$.

items.q: A freezer that is a reverse Carnot engine extracts $42\,\mathrm{kJ}$ as heat at $-15^\circ\mathrm{C}$ per cycle with coefficient of performance $5.7$. The room is at $30.3^\circ\mathrm{C}$. How much work does it need per cycle?
items.explain: $K=\dfrac{Q_L}{W}\Rightarrow W=\dfrac{42}{5.7}=7.4\,\mathrm{kJ}$. (Check: a Carnot refrigerator has $K=\dfrac{T_L}{T_H-T_L}=\dfrac{258.15}{45.3}=5.70$.)

items.q: That freezer extracts $42\,\mathrm{kJ}$ per cycle and needs $7.4\,\mathrm{kJ}$ of work. How much energy per cycle is delivered as heat to the room?
items.explain: Energy conservation for the refrigerator: $Q_H=Q_L+W=42+7.4=49.4\,\mathrm{kJ}$.

items.q: A refrigerator motor has a power of $200\,\mathrm{W}$. The freezing compartment is at $270\,\mathrm{K}$ and the outside air at $300\,\mathrm{K}$. Assuming a Carnot refrigerator, what is the maximum heat that can be extracted from the freezer in $10.0\,\mathrm{min}$?
items.explain:
$K=\dfrac{T_L}{T_H-T_L}=\dfrac{270}{30}=9.0$.
$Q_L=KW=9.0\times(200\,\mathrm{W}\times600\,\mathrm{s})=1.08\times10^{6}\,\mathrm{J}$.

items.q: A Carnot engine working between $T_1=400\,\mathrm{K}$ and $T_2=150\,\mathrm{K}$ drives a Carnot refrigerator working between $T_3=325\,\mathrm{K}$ and $T_4=225\,\mathrm{K}$. The engine absorbs $Q_1$ and the refrigerator delivers heat $Q_3$ to the $325\,\mathrm{K}$ reservoir. What is $Q_3/Q_1$?
items.explain:
Engine work: $W=\varepsilon Q_1=\left(1-\dfrac{150}{400}\right)Q_1=0.625\,Q_1$.
Refrigerator: $K=\dfrac{T_4}{T_3-T_4}=\dfrac{225}{100}=2.25$, so $Q_4=2.25W$ and $Q_3=Q_4+W=3.25W$.
$\dfrac{Q_3}{Q_1}=3.25\times0.625=2.03$.

items.q: Heat is transferred to a heat engine from a furnace at $80\,\mathrm{MW}$; waste heat is rejected to a river at $50\,\mathrm{MW}$. What are the net power output and thermal efficiency?
items.explain: Net power $=80-50=30\,\mathrm{MW}$; $\varepsilon=\dfrac{30}{80}=37.5\%$ (not $0.375\%$).

items.q: A car engine with a power output of $50\,\mathrm{kW}$ has a thermal efficiency of $24\%$. What is the fuel consumption rate if the fuel has a heating value of $44\,000\,\mathrm{kJ/kg}$?
items.explain:
Heat input rate $=\dfrac{50}{0.24}=208\,\mathrm{kW}$.
Fuel rate $=\dfrac{208.3}{44\,000}=4.73\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{kg/s}$.

items.q: A machine which does work using heat that flows spontaneously from a high-temperature source to a low-temperature sink is called a
items.explain: That is the definition of a heat engine (the Carnot engine is the ideal reversible case).

items.q: Which statement about entropy is true?
opts: It must stay constant in the universe
If it increases in one place, it must decrease elsewhere
If it decreases in one place, it must increase elsewhere (the total entropy of the universe cannot decrease)
It must decrease in the universe
items.explain: Second law: $\Delta S_{\text{universe}}\ge0$. A local decrease (a freezer, a living organism) is paid for by a larger increase somewhere else.

items.q: The efficiency of a heat engine is the ratio of
opts: the work done per cycle to the heat taken from the hot reservoir
the heat taken from the hot reservoir to the work done
the work done to the heat rejected to the cold sink
the heat rejected to the sink to the work done
items.explain: $\varepsilon=\dfrac{W}{Q_H}=\dfrac{\text{what you get}}{\text{what you pay}}$.

items.q: In a heat engine, the relationship between $Q_H$, $Q_L$ and the work $W$ is
items.explain: First law for a cycle: $W=|Q_H|-|Q_L|$.

items.q: An air conditioner supplies $1\,\mathrm{kg/s}$ of air at $15^\circ\mathrm{C}$, cooled from outside air at $35^\circ\mathrm{C}$ ($c_p=1.005\,\mathrm{kJ/(kg\,K)}$). Estimating it as a Carnot refrigerator, what power does it need?
items.explain:
Heat removed: $\dot Q_L=\dot mc_p\Delta T=1.005(20)=20.1\,\mathrm{kW}$.
Carnot $K=\dfrac{T_L}{T_H-T_L}=\dfrac{288.15}{20}=14.4$, so $\dot W=\dfrac{20.1}{14.4}=1.40\,\mathrm{kW}$.

items.q: A car engine has a thermal efficiency of $35\%$ and drives an air conditioner of coefficient of performance $3$. How much heat energy of fuel is needed to remove $1\,\mathrm{kJ}$ from the inside of the car?
items.explain:
Work needed: $W=\dfrac{Q_L}{K}=\dfrac13=0.333\,\mathrm{kJ}$.
Fuel energy $=\dfrac{W}{\varepsilon}=\dfrac{0.333}{0.35}=0.952\,\mathrm{kJ}$.

items.q: A cyclic machine receives $325\,\mathrm{kJ}$ from a $1000\,\mathrm{K}$ reservoir, rejects $125\,\mathrm{kJ}$ to a $400\,\mathrm{K}$ reservoir and produces $200\,\mathrm{kJ}$ of work. The cycle is
items.explain:
Its efficiency is $\dfrac{200}{325}=61.5\%$, which exceeds the Carnot limit $1-\dfrac{400}{1000}=60\%$.
Clausius check: $\sum\dfrac{Q}{T}=\dfrac{325}{1000}-\dfrac{125}{400}=+0.0125\,\mathrm{kJ/K}>0$, which violates the second law ($\oint\dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q}{T}\le0$). So the cycle is impossible.

items.q: The latent heat of fusion of ice is $80\,\mathrm{cal/g}$. What is the increase in entropy when one mole ($18\,\mathrm{g}$) of ice melts (in cal/(mol K))?
items.explain: $\Delta S=\dfrac{Q}{T}=\dfrac{80\times18}{273}=5.27\,\mathrm{cal/(mol\,K)}$.

items.q: What is the maximum possible efficiency (%) of a heat engine working between reservoirs at 500 K and 300 K?
items.explain: Carnot limit: $\varepsilon=1-\dfrac{T_L}{T_H}=1-\dfrac{300}{500}=40\%$.

items.q: $1000\,\mathrm{J}$ of heat flows spontaneously from a $500\,\mathrm{K}$ body to a $250\,\mathrm{K}$ body (both so large that their temperatures do not change). What is the total entropy change of the two bodies?
items.explain:
Hot body: $\Delta S_H=-\dfrac{1000}{500}=-2.0\,\mathrm{J/K}$; cold body: $\Delta S_L=+\dfrac{1000}{250}=+4.0\,\mathrm{J/K}$.
$\Delta S_{\text{total}}=+2.0\,\mathrm{J/K}>0$: the spontaneous (irreversible) process increases the entropy of the universe.

items.q: For a reversible cycle of an ideal engine, the total entropy change of the working gas over one cycle is
items.explain: Entropy is a state function, so over any complete cycle $\Delta S_{\text{gas}}=0$ (the surroundings gain entropy if the cycle is irreversible).

items.q: No heat engine can have an efficiency of 100% because of
opts: the second law of thermodynamics (Kelvin statement)
items.explain: Kelvin-Planck: no cyclic engine can convert heat from a single reservoir entirely into work. Even a frictionless engine must reject some heat to a cold sink.

items.q: Which has the larger coefficient of performance for the same temperatures, a Carnot refrigerator or any real refrigerator?
items.explain: Carnot's theorem: no refrigerator operating between two given reservoirs can have a larger coefficient of performance than a reversible one.
